MR. CHAIRMAN: Question No. 123. 
Loss of Revenue due to Ban on Smoking 
*123. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the total loss during the current year to the Government exchequer 
due to ban on smoking at public places an d ban on sponsorships of sporting 
events by tobacco firms;' and 
(b) in what manner Government propose to bridge the gap of revenue 
shortfall? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) Sir, The revenue Collection (which 
is mainly from central excise duty) in respect of tobacco products has shown 
an upward trend in the first quarter of the current financial year, as compared 
to the corresponding period last year. 
(b) Does not arise, in view of the above. 
(SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir, we all know that regulations on 
tobacco advertising and sponsorship of sports etc. are said to have hurt a 
section of business community. The Government put a ban on advertising 
and sponsoring sports events by tobacco firms, but the motive is defeated 
because major companies like ITC, Godfrey Phillips, VST, GTC etc. have 
already started setting-up of

RAJYA SABHA [31 July, 2001] 
surrogate brands to promote their flagship brands. I would like to know as to 
how the minister is going to deal with the situation. I demand that there 
should be a maximum excise duty on tobacco-related products. The Finance 
Bill, 2001 imposed, some additional levi es on cigarettes and tobacco-related 
products. The revenue, so collected, w ill go to the National Calamity Relief 
fund. I would like to know from the hon. Minister whether he would be kind 
enough to part with, at least, 15 per cent of the total revenue, so collected, for 
the welfare of the tobacco growers in the country, particularly in A.P. 
SHRI GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN: Sir, already, our Government 
has introduced a Bill to prohibit peop le who smoke at public places, from 
smoking at public places ...(Interruption)... It was referred to the Standing 
Committee, but it has yet not been legislated. We are waiting for the report of 
the committee. Except Delhi, Sikkim and Goa, no State in the country has 
enacted laws to prohibit people from smoking at public places. 
The hon. Member has also asked about the collection of revenue. Till now, 
there is no Central legislation to prohibit people from smoking at public 
places. Hence, it is not possible to quantif y the loss of revenue at this stage. 
Sir, in the financial year 2000-2001, up to June 2000, we had collected a total 
revenue of Rs. 1,133.11 crores from cigarettes. In the financial year 2001-
2002, up to June 2001, we have collected a total revenue of Rs. 1,201.58 
crores from cigarettes. Hence, there is no loss of revenue in respect of 
cigarettes. The Central Government has also imposed additional duties for 
the natural Calamity Relief Fund. 
Sir, we are collecting that amount for the natural Calamity Fund. The Hon. 
Member had asked whether this amount would be utilised for the welfare of 
the employees working in the cigare tte industry. The Government will 
examine his request. 
DR. Y. LAKSHMI PRASAD: He was talking about the tobacco growers. 
He had requested you to help the tobacco growers, not the company 
employees. 
SHRI   GINGEE   N.   RAMACHANDRAN:   Sir,   the   reply   is

DR. KARAN SINGH: Sir, the hon. Minister sounded somewhat apologetic 
about the fact that tobacco production was not going to fall. Cigarette 
smoking is one of the major health hazards in the world today. Lakhs of 
people die every year directly as a result of cigarette smoking. Any 
enlightened, Government would move towards a ban or maximum possible 
reduction of cigarette smoking. Sir, you might remember that when I was the 
Health Minister, we introduced a da nger sign on every packet. Now it is a 
farce. You go to any area in Delhi toda y. You will see huge advertisements 
glamorous boys and girls smoking and a tiny illegible thing written in one 
corner saying, "Cigarette smoking is dangerous". Sir, everybody knows that 
foreign companies are now dumping their cigarettes here in huge numbers. 
They give cigarettes free to the young people so that they become addicted. 
This is a major health hazard. I have all sympathy for the tobacco growers. I 
agree that some alternative proposal should be made for that. But, for the 
health of the nation, will the hon. Mini ster please assure the House that he 
would not look upon this as a financial resource? He may as well be making 
money out of dead bodies. This is a matter in which I feel a certain passion 
and a certain commitment is required.

*121. SHRIMATI SAROJ DUBEY: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of bilateral agreements which Air India entered with various 
airlines during the last two years;

of these bilateral agreements; 
(c) the details of seat adjustments utilized by Air India and other airlines; 
(d) whether it is a fact that the Air In dia lost a large number of seats of 
other airlines as a result thereof; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) 
and (b) Bilateral Air Services Agreemen ts are entered into by Governments 
and not airlines. Prior to 1999, India had finalised bilateral Air Services 
Agreements with 93 countries. Under

capacity entitlement for both countries. Prior to 1999, about 31.8 million

More rights to Malaysian Airlines 
*125. SHRI SHATRUGHAN SINHA: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Malaysian Airlines has been given more rights than they 
had asked for in bilateral airlines talks concluded some time back; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that Government had ordered an enquiry into this 
matter; and 
(d) if so, the findings thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) 
to (d) No, Sir. During the bilateral air services negotiations held in 
September, 2000 between Government of India and Government of 
Malaysia, Malaysian Government had requested a total increase of 4800 seats 
per week which was not agreed to and it was decided to increase the capacity 
entitlement for each side by 1500 seats only resulting in a total entitlement of 
3900 seats per week for each side. This  was done keeping in view the high 
seat factor of 84% of India-Malaysia route. Due to shortage of aircraft with 
national carriers, it was also agreed that Malaysian Airlines may operate 
additional 1200 seats per week against the unutilised capacity entitlement of 
the Indian side subject to commercial agreements with national carriers. 
Whenever our national carriers wish to operate these seats, Malaysian Airlines 
will have to withdraw accordingly. Till then the national carriers will gain 
financially by such utilisation of 
30 

[31 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Indian  entitlements by  Malaysian  Airlines.  Last enhancement of capacity 
was done in 1990. 
Operation of Malaysian Airlines to Mumbai was made conditional to their 
operation from the newly declared international airports of Bangalore and 
Hyderabad. In exchange, national carriers will also be able to operate to two 
additional tourist points of Malaysia, namely, Penang and Langkawi. 
Moreover, Indian side has also gain ed a connect code share arrangement 
from Mumbai, Bangalore and Hyderabad all the way to West Coast of USA 
through Kualalumpur with a facility to discharge and pickup passengers at 
Kualalumpur (5th freedom rights). Further, designated Airline of India shall 
be able to exercise 5th freedom tra ffic right from Kualatampur to Jakarta, 
Auckland in New Zealand and two points in Australia. 
In view of the above, the arrangement reached between India and Malaysia 
are quite balanced and satisfactory.

Loss suffered by AAI 
*136. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the observations of 
Comptroller and Auditor General of India regarding the loss suffered by Airports 
Authority of India in finalizing bids for awarding of a contract for running duty 
free shops; and 
(b) if so, what steps have been taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) 
and (b) The Comptroller and Auditor General, in its report has observed that the 
contracts for Duty Free Shops could not be awarded to highest bidder due to 
Management's lapse in inviting bids for running the Duty Free Shops departmental^ 
without having expertise for the same and obtaining financial bids in an erroneous 
manner from the existing parties for the original tender, and AAI had to forego 
a total revenue of Rs. 168.75 crores upto June, 2000. The facts of the matter in 
this regard are as under: 
In June, 1995, AAI had invited pre-qualification global tanders for selection of 
consultant/consolidators to assist the AAI to set up Duty Free Shopping 
Arcades in the additional areas identified at the five international airports of Delhi, 
Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata and Thiruvananthapuram. In January, 1996 a 
Committee felt that AAI did not have sufficient experience in the running of duty 
free shops. Therefore, the committee deci ded to select a concessionaire for 
running duty free shops and shortlisted four parties from the bids r eceived. 
Accordingly in August, 1996, AAI asked those shortlisted 
46 

[31 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
parties to submit financial bids. They were asked to submit bids for setting up duty 
free shops not only in the additional area identified in the begining at the five 
international airports but also in new Terminal-2C at Mumbai, which was under 
construction. In June 1996, broad terms and conditions were finalised. In August 
1996, financial bids were received. M/s Lion City Holding, Singapore bid 
highest for Terminal-2C while M/s Weitnaur Switzerland bid highest for 
additional area. All the bidders were asked to match with the highest offer in 
respect of the two segments. M/s Lion City Holding, who had been ranked 
higher in the technical presentation offered to hike their offer to match with M/s 
Weitnaur and were, therefore, asked to revalidate their Earnest Money 
Deposit (EMD). M/s Lion City did not revalidate their EMD and therefore 
their offer got invalidated. It was also decided to delink Terminal-2C at Mumbai 
as it was still under construction and also to consider the offer M/s Weitnaur. 
While negotiating the contract terms with M/s Weitnaur, AAI noticed some 
legal infirmity in tender procedures i.e. the pre-qualification for tenders 
invited in 1995 were for consultant/ consolidators to assist AAI, whereas the 
final proposed award was for concessionaire. In May, 1998 AAI took a decision 
to reject the tender due to this legal infirmity. If the tenders had been awarded, it 
would have led to legal complication and court cases.

all flood affected regions in various States.

the problem of floods in the country. The Rashtriya Barh Ayog (RBA) set up 
in 1976 examined the problem in detail and submitted its report in 1980. The 
recommendations of R.B.A. which form the framework for flood management 
strategy in the country, were forwarded to all the State Governments for 
implementation.

953. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that due to the present Export Import Policy, India 
will be a place for dumping ground; and

THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
MURASOLI MARAN): (a) and (b) The present five year Export and Import 
Policy was announced on 31.03.1997. India's export growth rate during 
1997-98 was 9.5% during 1998-99 was 7.4%, during 1999-2000 was 14.17% 
and was 26.39% in 2000-2001 (in rupee terms). Similarly, the growth rate of 
imports during this period was 11% in 1997-98, 14.2% in 1998-99, 13.6% in

73 

RAJYA SABHA [31 July, 2001]

apprehensions regarding India becoming a dumping ground are not borne 
out by facts. 
However, export promotion is a constant endeavour of the government and 
export growth is being constantly monitored. Export policy and strategy is 
formulated accordingly. In this direction, a number of steps have recently 
been taken. These include reduction in transaction cost through 
decentralization, simplification of proc edures and various other measures as 
enumerated in the Exim Policy. Steps have also been taken to promote 
exports through multilateral and bilateral initiatives. Further, Special 
Economic Zones (SEZ) are being set up to boost the exports. The measures 
announced, in amendments to Exim Policy, on 31.03.2001 include promotion 
of agricultural exports through setting up of Agri Export Zones, improvement 
in market access, setting up business- cum-trade facilitation centre and trade 
portal besides strengthening the present duty remission schemes like advance 
licence scheme, duty free replenishment certificate, duty entitlement 
passbook scheme etc.

AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN): (a) and (b) Following are the schemes being 
implemented by the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, Ministry of 
Commerce and Industry for the development of industrially backward areas in 
the country; 
(1) Growth Centre Scheme: 
Under this scheme 71 growth centres are proposed to be developed throughout 
the country which would be provided with basic infrastructure facilities like 
power, water, telecommunication, sewage, effluent disposal etc. enabling them to 
attract industries. The growth centres approved by the Government of India are to 
be developed by the State Governments with Central assistance of Rs. 10 crores 
per centre (Rs. 15 crores in the case of North-Eastern region). The scheme 
introduced during 1988 has been extended to the 9th Five Year Plan Period. 
(2) Transport Subsidy Scheme: 
This Scheme was introduced in July, 1971 to promote industries in hilly, remote 
and inaccessible areas. The scheme is applicable to the States of Himachal Pradesh, 
Jammu & Kashmir, the North-Eastern States, Sikkim, Union Territories of Andaman 
& Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep, Darjaling district of West Bengal and 
eight hill districts of Uttaranchal comprising Almora, Chamoli, Dehra dun, 
Nainital, Pauri Garhwal, Pithorgarh, Tehri-Garhwal and Uttar Kashi. Under the 
scheme, subsidy ranging from 50% — 90% is admissible of transport costs incurred 
on movement of raw materials and finished goods from designated rail heads 
/ports up to the location of industrial units and vice-versa for a period of five 
years from the date of commencement of commercial production. The scheme has 
been extended up to 31.3.2007.

Norms for Opening Post Offices 
1. Norms for opening Extra Departmental Branch Post Office: 
Population: In Normal Areas: 
3000 population in a group of villages [including the Proposed Post Office (PPO) 
village] 
In Hilly,  Tribal, Desert and Inaccessible Areas: 
500 population in an individual village or 1000 population in a group of 
villages. 
Distance: In Normal Areas: 
The minimum distance from the nearest existing post office will be 3 Kms. 
In Hilly,  Tribal, Desert and Inaccessible Areas: 
The distance limit will be the same as above except that in Hilly Areas, the 
minimum distance limit can be relaxed by the Directorate in cases where such 
relaxation is warranted by special circumstances which should be clearly 
explained while submitting a proposal. 
Anticipated Income: In Normal Areas: 
The Minimum anticipated revenue will be 33 1/3%  of the cost. 
In Hilly, Tribal, Desert and Inaccessible Areas: 
The minimum anticipated income will be 15% of the cost. 
2. Criteria for upgrading/opening Departmental Sub-Post Offices: 
(a) In Rural Areas: The minimum work-load of the Extra 
Departmental Branch Post Office, proposed to be upgraded, should 
be five hours per day. The permissible limit of annual loss is 
Rs. 2400/- in Normal Rural areas and Rs. 4800'- in Tribal and Hilly 
areas. 
(b) In Urban Areas: In Urban areas, the post office should initially 
be self-supporting, and, at the time of the first annual review, it 
should show a 5% profit to be eligible for further retention. 
The minimum distance between two post offices should be 1.5 Kms 
109 

RAJYA SABHA [31 July, 2001) 
in cities with a population of 20 lakhs and above, and 2 Kms. in other Urban 
Areas. No two delivery offices, however, should be closer than 5 Kms. for 
each other. 
Heads of Circles have powers to relax the distance condition in 10% of the 
cases. 
A Delivery Post Office in Urban Area should have a minimum of 7 
Postmen's beats.

COMMUNICATION (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) There have been no violation of the tender norms and no loss 
has been caused to the Government on account thereof. The Notice inviting 
Tender (NIT) for induction of additional cellular operators in various service 
areas in the country was floated on 9.3.2001. The pre-qualification bids

were evaluated in accordance with the conditions prescribed in the tender 
document. 
The eligibility criteria as contained in Clasue 5.1 (vi) of the Tender 
Document provided that "Any number of Indian Companies as well as foreign 
Companies may join together to promote the joint venture bidder company. 
However, an Indian company or a foreign company cannot be part of more 
than one such joint venture bidder company. The same Indian company in its 
sole capacity can bid either by itself or through its joint venture company." 
While evaluating the pre-qualification bids it was found that two Reliance 
group companies namely, M/s. Reliabl e Internet Services Limited and 
Reliance Communications Private Limited had submitted 
118 

[31 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
their bids for 15 Service Areas each. Fo rm the equity structure of these two 
companies, it was found that none of their partners arc common and as such 
there was no violation to the eligibility criteria prescribed in the Tender 
Document. However, in order to ensure fair competition, all the bidders were 
asked to confirm that there is no common interest of any of the 
partners/promoters/constituents in any other bidding company who has bid 
for the same service area and in case their is any common interest, only on 
bid for a service area shall be consider ed. They were given option to retain 
only such bids so as to ensure fair competition. In response to this, M/s. 
Reliance Communications Private Limited chose to withdraw all the bids 
submitted by them for 15 Circles. This was allowed to the company. The 
Earnest Money Bank Guarantee (EMBG) and Financial Bids were returned 
to the company before the first stage Financial Bids were scheduled to the 
opened. Withdrawal of the bids by M/s Reliance Communications settled the 
matter. Allowing both the bids would have given rise to unfair competition 
leading to subsequent stages of financial bidding as infructuous. EMBG can 
not be forfeited in the situation where a bidder is disqualified in the pre-
qualification stage or opted to withdraw the bids in terms of option given by 
the Government. 
(d) Docs not arise in view of (b) and (c) above.

second report relating to capital restructuring and reforms was submitted in 
July, 2001. 
152 

[31 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
The main features of the scheme recommended by the Expert Group for 
one time settlement of outstanding dues are a$ under:— 
(a) 50 per cent waiver of surcharge/interest on delayed payments; 
(b) For the remaining dues i.e. the entire principle outstanding as well as 
the remaining 50% surcharge, bonds could be issued by the respective State 
Governments; 
(c) The bonds could be issued through RBI at a tax free interest rate of 
8.5%; 
(d) The bonds should be structured to achieve a moratorium of 5 years on 
repayment of principle with the entire principle being repaid between the 6th 
and 15th year; 
(e) the bonds shall be identical to bonds issued in connection with the 
market borrowings of State Governments, with the attendant discipline in 
repayments. The bonds will be subject to lock-in-restrictions that will allow 
release of only 10 per cent of the bonds in the secondary market each year; 
(f) For ensuring timely payment of current dues in future, defaults in 
current payment for power/fuel should  attract a graded reduction in the 
supply of power from central power stations and in coal supplies. Where 
such defaults exceed 90 days from the date of billing the Ministry of Finance 
should recover these dues through adjustment against releases due to them 
from the Centre; 
(g) As part of the scheme, SEBs should accept, reform-based 
performance milestones such a setting up of SERCs, metering of 
distribution feeders and improvement in revenue realization. The 
milestones should be specified in the MOUs to be signed with the 
Ministry of Power; 
(h) The states should be offered incentives for complying with the scheme. 
If SEBs do not default on their current dues and adhere to the performance 
milestones, CPSUs should pay them, during the first four years commencing 
from 1.4.2001, bi-annual incentives equal to 2 per cent of the value of bonds; 
(i) Further, if SEBs open and ma intain LCs till the end of December, 
2001, CPSUs should pay them a one time cash incentive 
153 

RAJYA SABHA [31 July, 2001] 
equal to 2 per cent of the value of bonds; 
(j) In addition, States undertaking reforms should also be assisted through APDP 
grants and discretionary allocation of Power; 
(k) This scheme should enter into force only after one-half of the States that 
have an annual billing of over Rs. 500 crore per annum from CPSUs give their 
consent, and should be effective in respect of the States that give such consent; 
and 
(1) The States that withhold their consent beyond 60 days after this scheme 
enters into force should be  denied any share in the discretionary allocation of 
15 per cent from the Power stations of CPSUs as well as any assistance under 
APDP. If the overdues of such States exceeded to Rs. 50 crores in respect of any 
CPSU, they should also attract reduction in power and coal supplies, as applicable to 
the States participating in this scheme. 
Following the submission of the Report of the Expert Group a high level 
Empowered Group consisting of Finance Minister, Dy. Chairman, Planning 
Commission, Minister of Power and Chief Ministers of some States met on 
26.6.2001 and 6.7.2001. The Empowered Group endorsed the 
recommendations of the Expert Group with the following modifications:— 
(i) Waiver of surcharge would now be 60% instead of 50% as recommended 
by the Group; and 
(ii) The incentives for achieving the reform based milestones should be 
increased to 6% in the first year and 5% in the second year. 
Recently, Minister of Power has written to Chief Minister of States and 
UTs urging them to initiate necessary steps for implementation of the scheme 
at the earliest.

set of brokers and sub-brokers acting on behalf of a common set of clients who

Executive Director was also debarred from holding public office in any capital 
market related public institution for a period of three years. In the third phase, 
investigations were completed against Harshad Mehta, BPL, Videocon and 
Sterlite by October, 1999. Show cause notices were issued to them in 
December, 1999. The parties were given opportunity of final hearings in the 
month of March/April 2001. Pursuant to the hearings, SEBI passed orders on

proceedings through some of their directors/officials were ordered under section

Dandewala gas field. Out of the two we lls drilled, one was dry and the other

areas, as also explore in the deeper layers of the producing fields.

new technologies for seismic surveys, work over, stimulation 
operations, drilling of wells etc. in producing areas. 
In any field, generally a combination of various efforts are implemented 
simultaneously and' thus it is difficult to attribute oil gain to any individual

Protection of Jorhat District of Assam from Brahmaputra River 
1081. SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN:  Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) what action has been taken by Government to protect the North-Eastern 
Part of Jorhat District from the Brahmaputra; 
(b) how much fund had been released for the purpose and how was it utilised; 
(c) what is the new proposal about funding; and 
(d) whether Government would undertaken the work directly? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) To protect North 
Eastern part of Jorhat district from flood and erosion 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [31 July, 2001] 
of river Brahmaputra, the State Govt, of Assam has undertaken 7 nos. flood 
management schemes on south bank of river Brahmaputra and for protection 
of Majuli island a total estimated cost of Rs. 44.66 crore. 
The Brahmaputra Board under this Ministry has prepared Master Plan of Majuli 
island in which different long term measures for protection of Majuli island from 
flood and erosion of Brahmaputra have been identified. Based on the Master 
Plan, a detailed project report for protection of Majuli island from erosion of 
river Brahmaputra has been prepared by  Brahmaputra Board at an estimated 
cost of Rs. 243.64 crore. 
(b) Flood Management being a State subject, flood control projects are planned, 
funded and executed by the State Governments themselves out of their own 
resources and as per their own priorities. The assistance as being rendered by the 
Central Government are technical, catalytical and promotional in nature. The 
Central Government has been extending Central Loan, Assistance to the State 
Govt, of Assam since 1972—74 onwards. An amount of Rs. 390.94 crore as 
loan and Rs. 10.09 crore as Grant-in-aid have been released to the State Govt, 
of Assam upto March, 2000. An amount of Rs. 1.31 crore has been released by 
the State Govt, of Assam during 2000-2001 by undertaking the about mentioned 
six nos. short term flood management schemes in the North-Eastern part of Jorhat 
district. 
(c) A Centrally Sponsored for funding the flood control schemes in 
Brahmaputra and Barak basis with 90% Central share as grant and 10% State share 
is presently under the consideration of the Full Planning Commission. The 
Planning Commission also releases the funds to the North-Eastern States for 
various schemes under Non-lapsable Central Pool of Resources. 
(d) No, Sir.

Workshop on International Water Management 
1083. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: WUI the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the outcome of the three day International workshop in 
International Water Management recently held in Bangalore; 
(b) whether Government propose to fonnulate National Water 
Policy; and 
206 

[31 July, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) if so, by when the policy is likely to be formulated and announced? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) A three day 
International Workshop on Integrated Water Management was held on 21—23 
June, 2001 at Bangalore. The important outcomes of the workshop are: to 
provide opportunities for an open dialogue among water planners and managers and 
communities in attempting to manage water resources; to share successful water 
resources management experiences a nd technologies for dissemination of 
information; capacity building for Integrated Water Resources Management 
(IWRM); to define strategies for the future to be taken by governments, 
academics and NGOs towards sustainable and integrated water resources 
management planning and action; and sustainable action projects implementing 
principles of IWRM. 
(b) and (c) The National Water Policy has been adopted in September, 
1987 by the National Water Resources Council (NWRC) headed by the Prime 
Minister with Chief Ministers of all the States, Chief Ministers/Administrators of 
Union Territories and Union Ministers of water related Ministries as members.

TRIBUTES TO SHAHEED UDHAM SINGH 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, today is the anniversary of the 
martyrdom of Shaheed Udham Singh, who was hanged this day, 61 years ago, 
for killing Sir Michael O'Dwyer, who was Governor of Punjab when the 
Jalianwala Bagh firing took place on Ba isakhi day in 1919. Shri Udham 
Singh sacrificed his life for the Honour of his country and his contribution to 
inspiring the youth of the country and for attainment of India's freedom will 
always be remembered. It is because of  the sacrifices of  martyrs like Udham 
Singh that India is, today, an independent nation. Let us pay our respectful 
homage to his sacred memory. 
I request Members to rise in thei r places and observe silence in the 
memory of Shaheed Udham Singh.

SHRI YASHWANT SINHA: As I go along in my reply. I shall try 
to deal with various points which have been raised by the hon. Members in 
this House. But I would like to begin by putting forth certain facts in proper 
perspective with regard to the UTI and with regard to the US-64 Scheme. The 
first and the most important issue -- because this is something which has been 
raised in this House and outside -- is the issue of what happened to the money 
of the US-64 Scheme. A general impression has been created as if this money 
had vanished somewhere and that some people have pocketed this money and 
that it was not available. Let me ha sten to add that what actually has 
happened was that the value of the stocks held under US-64 Scheme has 
declined. So. the overall value of the fund has declined. It still has a corpus. It 
still has a value. As we go along, I am quite sure, it will achieve the levels 
which it had before the 30th June this year. 
We have, that is, the UTI has, come out with a redemption scheme 
which will be operational from tomorrow. And we have said that the 
Government stands fully behind the UTI. as far as the redemption or even a 
better redemption in future is concerned. So, nothing has happened to the 
corpus. It is not that somebody has walked away with it. It is only that its 
value has declined because its value is su bject to the fluctuations of the stock 
market. Now, why is it subject to the fluctuations of the stock market, Sir? It 
is subject to the fluctuations of the st ock market because, over a period of 
time, this fund, the US-64, became largely an equity fund. What is the nature 
of this US-64? It is not an assured-income scheme. But it is a regular income 
scheme. There are three features which distinguish this scheme. 
The first is, people who invest in the units 'Gt US-64 make capital 
gains. They purchase at a price and sell at a price which is higher. Secondly, 
they receive annual dividend from the UT I. And thirdly, it provides liquidity. 
It is almost like cash because, if you are holding units, you can go to the UTI 
offices, tender your units and get money for it. So, liquidity is a very, very 
important feature of this particular scheme. When the UTI announced the 
freeze on the 2 nd of July, it is this part wh ich suffered a major set back, 
namely, the liquidity of the scheme was supposed to be restricted for a period 
of six months, which the investors did not like, and a situation arose which 
we are now trying to correct.

*141. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO:  Will the Minister of TOURISM

THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI ANANTH 
KUMAR): (a) and (b) The Department of Archaeology and Museums, Govt, 
of Andhra Pradesh carried out a minor excavation and exploration at 
Geesukonda in district Warangal, AP, in November-December 2000. The 
excavation is reported to have yiel ded archaeological material comprising 
polished stone axes, iron objects, sling balls, foundation of a brick-built 
circular structure, terracotta figurines, beads and bangles, Satavahana and 
Vishnukundi coins. These finds range from Neolithic period to the 4th 
century A.D.

the excavated material has been chemically cleaned and preserved.

Deployment of Special Service Battalion along Indo-Nepal Border 
*148. DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR : Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has decided to deploy a Special Service Battalion 
of a Special Police Organisation along Indo-Nepal border in Bihar to control 
trans-border activities, including smuggling and I.S.I, activities; 
(b) whether this has been done after some anti-national activities came to 
Government's notice; and 
(c) if so, the details of such activities? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Of late, Indo-Nepal border has emerged as a vital link in 
Pakistans prolonged low intensity proxy war against India. Pak ISI  has been 
misusing this open border for launching major terrorist offensives against 
India. Militants from Kashmir and Punjab also continue to take shelter in 
Nepal and there is a growing nexus between militants/anti-India elements 
based in Nepalese territory with their counterparts on the Indian side of the 
border. This is in addition to other trans-border criminal activities like 
smuggling of contraband, explosives and fake Indian currency for which this 
border has been used for quite some time.

Laying of roads and development of watersheds in villages 
*149. SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether schemes relating to laying of roads and development of 
watersheds in villages are decided by Union Government; and 
(b) if so, the reasons for not consulting the State Governments to accord 
priority in their development? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M. VENKAIAH 
NAIDU): (a) and (b) The Rural Roads projects under the Pradhan Mantri 
Gram Sadak Yojana are formulated by the State Governments, keeping in 
view the Guidelines issued under the Programme. The projects are executed 
by the State authorities, after clearance of the same in the Government of 
India. 
Projects relating to Watersheds are covered under three Programmes viz. 
the Integrated Wastelands Development Programme (IWDP), the Drought 
Prone Areas Programme (DPAP) and the Desert Development Programme 
(DDP). Under the IWDP, the projects are sanctioned by the Department of 
Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Deve lopment, after their prioritization in 
consultation with the concerned State Governments. As regards the DPAP 
and the DDP, the Government of India decide the number of new projects to 
be sanctioned to a Programme District, keeping in view the Annual Budget 
Allocation as well as the performance of the District in the execution of 
ongoing Watershed Projects. The exact location of the projects is determined 
by the concerned DRDAs/Zilla Panchayats, in consultation with the State 
Governments.

Need for Global look for Indian Textile Industry 
*152. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government have deci ded to face the challenges of the 
rapidly changing world textiles scenario by stressing the need for Indian 
Textile Industry to consider itself as operating in a global market; 
(b) if so, to what extent, the textile industry has changed its course for 
operating in a global market; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI KASHIRAM RANA): (a) to (c) 
The Government is fully committed to face the challanges of globalisation by 
encouraging investments for modernisation and upgradation of the textile 
industry. 
The National Textile Policy-2000 (NTxP-2000), provides an enabling 
environment to make the domestic text ile industry strong enough to face 
growing global competition. De-reservation of the woven segment of 
readymade garment sector will allow the industry to achieve desired 
economies of scale. In order to implement the vision of the NTxP-2000, a 
"Textile Package" was announced in the Budget 2001-02 to encourage 
investment in the textile sector. Some of the important provisions of the 
"Textile Package" are:—  
(i) Customs duty has been reduced from 15% to 5% on 159 specified 
textile and garment machineries. In addition, 12 important items of 
machineries including shuttleless looms have also been exempted 
from additional excise duty. 
40 

[1st August 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
A programme has been announced to induct 50,000 shuttleless 
looms and to modernise 2.5 lakh powerlooms in the decentralised 
sector by 2004. 
(ii) Assistance under Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) 
providing for a reimbursement of 5% out of interest, is available 
to the textile industry for modernisation and upgradation. In 
addition, rate of depreciation allowance for machinery under 
TUFS has been raised to 50%. 
(iii) A provision of Rs. 10 cror es has been earmarked in the B udget 
2001-02 for the establishment of Apparel Parks for production 
and export of garments. Besides a provision of Rs. 15 crores has 
been made for the Scheme for improvement of critical 
infrastructure facilities at major textile production centres. 
In addition, a Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC) with an outlay of 
about Rs. 600 crores has been launched by the Government to improve the 
productivity and quality of cotton required by the textile industry.

(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M. VENKAIAH 
NAIDU): (a) At present, no such large scale scarcity of potable water has been 
reported by the State Governments. However, reports have been received 
from Karnataka and Maharashtra about deficient rainfall during the current monsoon 
and consequent scarcity of drinking water in some parts of these States. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
50 

[1st August 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Central teams have been deputed to visit these States to study the situation. 
Recently, a report regarding scarcity of drinking water has also been received 
from the State of Andhra Pradesh. 
(b) to (d) So far as rural drinking water supply is concerned, it is a State 
subject. However, the Government of India supplements the efforts of the 
States by providing financial assistance on matching basis under the 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Pr ogramme (ARWSP). Funds are also 
provided to the States under the Rural Drinking Water Component of the 
Prime Minister's Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY). Powers have been delegated 
to the State Governments to plan, approve and implement projects under 
ARWSP and PMGY—Rural Drinking Water Supply.  
In order to supplement the efforts of State Governments in providing .water 
in small towns having population less than 20,000, Government of India is 
implementing Accelerated Urban Wa ter Supply Programme under which 
funds are provided by the Centre to the State Governments on a 50:50 
matching basis. 
States themselves plan and implement schemes to meet the drinking water 
scarcity. However, to review the overa ll drought situation and coordinate the 
mitigation efforts, Government of India has constituted a Management Group 
under the Chairmanship of Cabinet Secr etary. Further, a Group of Ministers 
(GoM) under the Chairmanship of Finance Minister has also been functioning 
to reveiw and monitor the drought mitigation efforts. 
After the monsoon season of last year (2000), scarcity of drinking water 
due to deficient rainfall was reported from 8 States of Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, 
Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, Rajasthan and 
Uttaranchal. In view of the scarcity of  drinking water then prevailing in rural 
areas of these States on account of drought, the priorities fixed in the 
Guidelines had been relaxed up to June 30, 2001 by the Government of India 
to the extent that the funds under ARWSP and PMGY—Rural Drinking 
Water could also be utilised for activities  relating  to  repair,   rejuvenation,  
renovation,  restoratior 
51 

RAJYA SABHA [1st August 2001] 
and replacement of existing rural drinking water systems in areas affected by 
scarcity of drinking water in these 8 States, including Gujarat. 
In case of Gujarat, during the year 2000-2001 under ARWSP (including 
ARWSP-DDP), Rs. 74.85 crores were a llocated to the State and keeping in 
view the drought situation prevailed in the State, the entir e allocation of Rs. 
74.85 crores was released by relaxing the conditions laid down for release of 
funds. In the wake of the earthquake and drought in the State, an additional 
Rs. 100.00 crores was provided to the State under ARWSP for rural drinking 
water supply.

Report on the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 has recommended, inter alia, 
insertion of a new sub-section, 1(A), in section 164 to read as follows:

Law Commission in the 154th Report, in entirety, after consulting State 
Governments and other concerned organisations.

the issue of seismic safety of Tehri Dam. This Group in its report concluded

tenure of the Committee upto 14.8.2001 to enable the Committee finalize its

Electrification of villages in Arunachal Pradesh 
1149. SHRI NABAM REBIA: Will the Mi nister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Central Government have formulated any concrete scheme 
for electrification of the villages in the State of Arunachal Pradesh; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the details of villages in the State that have been electrified, so 
far; and 
(d) by when, all the villages of State are likely to be electrified? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (d) Rural Electrification has 
now been included under Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY). 
Finance Minister in his Speech while presenting the Union Budget for 
2001-2002 has announced that a package of initiatives is being launched by 
the Government to improve the power distribution system in rural areas. This 
includes: 
120 

[1st August 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(i)  Completion  of electrification  of bulk  of the   remaining villages 
in the next six years. 
(ii) Extension of assistance to the States for village electrification works 
under the Prime Minister's Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY) whose 
funding is being augmented. 
(iii) Stepping up credit support from  Rural Electrification Corporation 
to SEBs for speedy electrification of dalit bastis; households of 
scheduled tribes and other weaker sections of society; 
(iv) Improving the quality of power supply in villages. 
(v) Augmentation of distribution networks in rural areas supported by 
REC under the Accelerated Power Development Programme 
(APDP). 
(vi) Earmarking a sum of Rs. 750 crores out of RIDF by allowing it to 
float capital gains tax exemption bonds along with NABARD and 
NHAl under Section 54 EC of the Income Tax Act.

Lapsable Central Pool of Resources. 
Government have set the goal of 100% electrification of villages feasible to 
be connected with the Grid by 2007. Th e remote villages are proposed to be 
electrified using non-conventional sources of energy by the year 2012.

Electrification of villages through renewable energy sources 
1156. SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister of 
POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have fixed a goal of generating 10 per cent share 
in the additional power generation by the year 2012 which would work out to 
10,000 MW; 
(b) whether Government have also devised an action plan to electrify 
80,000 villages over the next seven years through renewable energy sources; 
and 
(c) if so, what steps are being taken to achieve both the targets? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) Based on the findings of the 
16th Electric Power Survey, it has been estimated that an additional capacity 
of 1,07,000 MW is required to be added by 2012 to meet the energy 
requirement of 975 BUs. The Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources 
have prepared a Draft Renewable Energy Policy Statement which envisages 
10% or 10,000 MW of the add itional planned capacity to come from non-
conventional energy sources by the year 2012. 
There are about 79,000 villages as on 1.4.2001 which remain to be electrified 
in the country. Out of this, about 18,000 villages are in remote and in 
difficult areas. The Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources proposes 
to implement a programme for electrification of villages in remote and 
difficult areas in the country 
136 

[1st August 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
during the next 10-11 years. Consultations have been held with State 
Governments, NGOs, financial institutions and manufacturers to develop an 
action plan for this purpose. State Governments have been asked to send lists 
of un-electrified villages which cannot be electrified by conventional means. 
A provision of Rs. 20 crores has been included in the budget of the Ministry 
for 2001-02 to initiate implementation of this programme. 
Filling up the post of CMD, in NEEPCO 
1157. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Nort h Eastern Electric Power Corporation 
(NEEPCO) is running with an ad-hoc CMD; 
(b) whether key posts in the Board- of  Directors are lying vacant with 
many of the Directors due to retire soon; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the action taken to fill up these key posts for better functioning of 
NEEPCO in the light of news-item in Assam Tribune dated 8th July, 2001 
captioned "Outstanding dues posing problems for NEEPCO"? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (d) The posts of Chairman & 
Managing Director and Director (Finance), North Eastern Electric Power 
Corporation (NEEPCO) fell vacant with effect from 1.11.2000 and 1.3.2001 
respectively consequent upon the retir ement of respective incumbents. The 
delay in the filling up these posts wa s on account of consultation process 
related certain administrative procedures and late receipt of requisite 
information and documents from the respective organizations where the 
selected candidates arc employed. Thes e cases have since been processed 
and on receipt of the approval of the Competent Authority, the posts of CMD 
Director (F), NEEPCO would be filled.

One-time settlement formula for SEBs outstanding dues 
1158. SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: 
 SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY:  
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether some States have approached the Union Government to provide 
more time to study the proposed one-time settlement formula for the State 
Electricity Boards outstanding dues; 
(b) if so, the States that have made such a request and the total amount of 
dues, State-wise; 
(c) the details of the penalties imposed by the Union Government and the. 
reaction of the State Governments; and 
(d) what final decision has been taken by Union Government for the 
settlement of the dues? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) Recently Minister of Power has written to 
Chief Ministers of States and UTs urging them to initiate steps for 
implementation of the one time Scheme of settlement of outstanding dues of State 
Electricity Boards. Response to Minister of Power's letter is awaited. Statement 
of outstanding dues payable to CPSUs of Ministry of Power as on 30.4.2001 is 
given in the Statement (See below). 
(c) and (d) The scheme proposed by the Expert Group on one time settlement of 
dues of SEBs has many incentives and some penalties. The details of the scheme 
recommended by the Expert Group are as under: 
(a) The Group recommended 50 per cent waiver of surcharge/  
interest on delayed payments. 
(b) For the remaining dues i.e. the entire principal outstanding as well as the 
remaining 50% surcharge, bonds would be issued by the respective 
State Governments. 
(c) The bonds would be issued through RBI at a tax free interest rate of 
8.5% p.a. 
138 

[1st August 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) The bonds should be structured to achieve a moratorium of 5 years on 
repayment of principal with the entire principal being repaid between 
the 6th and 15th year. 
(c) These bonds shall be identical to bonds issued in connection with the 
market borrowings of State Governments, with the attendant discipline in 
repayments. The bonds will be subject to lock-in restrictions that will 
allow release of only 10 per cent of the bonds in the secondary market 
each year. 
(f) For ensuring timely payment of current dues in future, defaults in 
current payment for power/fuel should attract a graded reduction in the 
supply of power from central power stations and in coal supplies. Where 
such defaults exceed 90 days from the date of b illing, the Ministry of 
Finance should recover these dues through adjustment against releases 
dues to them from the Centre. 
(g) As part of the scheme, SEBs should accept reform-based performance 
milestones such as setting up SERCs, metering of distribution feeders 
and improvement in revenue realisation. The milestones should be 
specified in the MOUs to be signed with the Ministry of Power. 
(h) The States should be offered incentives for complying with the 
scheme. If SEBs do not default on their current dues and adhere to the 
performance milestones, CPSUs should pay them, during the first 
four years commencing from 1.4.2001, bi-annual cash incentives 
equal to 2 per cent of the value of bonds. 
(i) Further, if SEBs open and maintain LCs till the end of December, 2001, 
CPSUs should pay them a one-time cash incentive equal to 2 per cent 
of the value of bonds. 
(j) In addition, States undertaking reforms should also be assisted thro ugh 
APDP grants and discretionary allocation of power. 
(k) This scheme should enter into force only after one-half of 
139 

RAJYA SABHA [1st August 2001] 
the States that have an annual billing of over Rs. 500 crore per annum 
from CPSUs give their consent, and should be effective in respect of 
the States that give such consent. 
(1) The States that withhold their consent beyond 60 days after this 
scheme enters into force should be denied any share in the 
discretionary allocation of 15 per cent from the power stations of 
CPSUs as well as any assistance unde r APDP. If the ovcrducs of such 
States exceeded Rs. 50 crores in respect of any CPSU, they should also 
attract reduction in power and coal supplies, as applicable to the States 
participating in this scheme. 
Following the submission of the Report of the Expert Group a high level 
Empowered Group consisting of Finance Minister, Dy. Chairman, Planning 
Commission, Minister of Power and Chief Ministers of some States met on 
26.6.2001 and 6.7.2001. The Empowered Group endorsed the 
recommendations of the Expert Group with the following modifications: 
(i) Waiver of surcharge would now be 60% instead of 50%  as 
recommended by the Group. 
(ii) The incentives for achieving th e reform-based milestones shall be 
increased to 6% in the first year and 5% in the second year.

Allocation of l/3rd of the total capacity of Anta Gas Power Station to 
Rajasthan 
1160. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Rajasthan used to enjoy a sp ecial allocation of l/3rd of total 
capacity in NTPC's Anta Gas Power Station since 1993 but the same was 
suddenly withdrawn by Government on 29th October, 1999; 
(b) whether the State Government has taken up this matter with the 
Ministry of Power vide letter dated 13th December, 1999; 
(c) if so, what steps till date have been taken by Government to restore the 
special allocation of l/3rd of the total capacity of Anta Gas based Power 
Station to Rajasthan; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) As a special case, l/3rd out-put of 
Anta GPS was allocated to Rajasthan w.e.f, from October 1993, due to acute 
power shortage condition then prevailing in the State. This special allocation 
was continued due to prolonged outage of units of 1 & 2 of the Rajasthan 
Atomic Power Station (RAPS) with effect from February, 1994 and August, 
1994 respectively. The Unit-1 of RAPS was restored in April, 1997 and Unit-
2 in June, 1998. Consequent to restoration of units 1 & 2 of RAPS and 
persistent pressure from the other constituent States of Northern Region for 
restoration of their entitled shares in Anta GPS, this special allocation to 
Rajasthan had to be withdrawn in October, 1999.

Rajasthan for restoration of the special allocation of one-third out-put from 
Anta GPS. The Anta GPS (419 MW) is a regional power station and all the 
constituent Statcs-UTs of Northern Region have firm shares in the power 
station in accordance with the sharing fo rmula. Therefore, restoration of the 
special allocation to Rajasthan would de prive  the  other States in  the 
Northern  Region  of their

entitled   shares   and   likely  to  attract  stiff opposition  from   other

Arsenic poisoning of ground water in West Bengal 
1166. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have decided to stop funding 
under the special Centrally sponsored scheme in West Bengal 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
158 

[1st August 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
for tackling the problem of arsenic poisoning of the ground water in vast 
stretches of the State; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(c) whether this is to imply that the dimension of the problem has been 
reduced substantially, so much so, that it does not further warrant any 
Central support? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) No, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Rural drinking water supply is a State subject. State 
Governments take up schemes/projects for providing drinking water in rural 
areas from their own resources. Government of India supplements the efforts 
of the State Governments and provide financial assistance under Accelerated 
Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP) and Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya 
Yojana (PMGY)— Rural Drinking Water (RDW). Under ARWSP, up to 
20% of the allotted funds can be utilised to tackle water quality problem 
which inter-alia includes providing safe drinking water free from arsenic 
contamination and sustainability of sources. As reported by the Government 
of West Bengal, as on 1.4.1999, out of  total 79,036 rural habitations in the 
State 3,133 habitations are affected with arsenic contamination. 
To tackle arsenic contamination in drinking water, prior to 1.4.1998, under 
Sub-Mission programme of ARWSP, 3 projects were sanctioned to West 
Bengal at a total approved cost of Rs. 259.79 crore, out of which 
Government of India's share is about Rs. 194.84 crore and State share is Rs. 
64.95 crore. So far Government of India has released Rs. 180.13 crore. 
Remaining funds Rs. 14.71 crore will be released on the basis of the progress 
of implementation and fulfillment of conditions laid down for the released of 
funds. Since 
159 

RAJYA SABHA [1st August 2001] 
1.4.1998, powers to plan, approve and implement schemes under Sub-
Mission have been delegated to the States. States can also take up 
schemes/projects to provide safe drinking water under PMGY-RDW and 
powers to approve schemes/projects have been delegated to State 
Governments. During 2000-2001, Rs. 78.37 crore under ARWSP and Rs. 
58.74 crore under RDW component of PMGY were released. For the current 
year, Rs. 43.86 crore under ARWSP and Rs. 9.40 crore under RDW 
component of PMGY have been released as 1st installment. 
Keeping in view the problem of arsenic contamination in ground water in 
the State, as a special case, instead of 20%, 50% of ARWSP funds have been 
allowed to be spent on tackling arsenic contamination in 24 North Parganas 
District. As per information received from the Government of West Bengal, 
after 1.4.1998, during 2000-2001, State Government has sanctioned two 
projects—one project in Nort h 24 Parganas District at a total cost of Rs. 
124.82 crore covering 318 habitations under ARWSP and another project in 
Malda district at a total cost of Rs . 43.00 crore covering 367 habitations 
under PMGY—Rural Drinking Water, for tackling arsenic problem in 
drinking watet. 
National conference of Panchayat Raj State Ministers 
1167. SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN: SHRI 
N.R. DASARI: 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a national conference of the Panchayat Raj 
State Ministers was held in Delhi recently; and 
(b) if so, the details of the subjects discussed therein and the outcome 
thereof? 
160 
 

[1st August 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M. VENKAIAH 
NAIDU): (a) Yes, Sir. A Conference of  State Ministers of Panchayati Raj 
was held on 11.07.2001 at New Delhi. 
(b) The subjects discussed and broad consensus arrived at in the 
conference are given in the Statement (See below) 
Statement 
Major recommendations of the Conference of State Ministers of 
Panchayati Raj held on 11.07.2001 at New Delhi 
The following resolutions/recommendations on strengthening of 
Panchayati Raj Institutions were adopted unanimously by the State Ministers 
of Panchayati Raj present in the Conference. 
(i) Elections—  
 It was agreed that since the holding of Panchayat elections every 5 years 
is mandatory, State Governments/Union Territory Administration shall 
ensure that elections are held with the same regularity with which 
Parliament and Assembly elections are held. 
 States/UTs should refrain from  approaching Law Courts for 
postponement of elections. While the adequacy of the legal provisions 
pertaining to Panchayat elections  can be examined, the State 
Governments have to, in the first instance, ensure regular holding of 
elections. 
 It was desirable of Panchayat elections to be held on non-party basis. 
 The process of delimitation of constituencies and reservation of seats for 
SCs/STs and women should be settled well in advance, for giving 
sufficient opportunity for settling disputes, if any, on these issues. 
 If Panchayat elections are not held on time, the Planning 
Commission/Government of India can issue directions for withholding 
funds under Central Schemes/Centrally Sponsored Schemes. 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [1st August 2001] 
(ii) Devolution of funds, functions and functionaries upon PRIs—  
 It was agreed that States/UTs would devolve functions upon PRIs in 
respect of the subjects listed in the XI schedule and issue detailed 
executive instructions devolving specific and substantial executive 
powers upon each tier of' Panchayats by 31.3.2002. 
 A Task Force comprising senior officers of the Ministry of Rural 
Development and of the State Governments will be set up at the earliest 
to operationalise administrative decentralization of funds, functions 
and functionaries with regard to the subjects in the Constitution, so 
that functional and financial devolution is completed by 31st March, 
2002. 
 Incentives should be extended to the Panchayats by the State 
Governments by way of grants-in-aids for their better performance as 
regards raising their own resources. 
 Panchayats may be given untied funds to enable them to select 
development work according to their needs. 
(iii) Constitution of DPCs—  
 The Conference, taking note of the poor progress in setting up of 
District Planning Committees in  most of the States/UTs, 
recommended that these be constituted by the end of 2001. 
 It was agreed that the practice of  appointing Minister-in-charge of 
district as Chairperson of DPC should be discontinued and that the 
Chairman of District Panchayat o ught to be the Chairperson of the 
DPC. 
(iv) Strengthening of Gram Sabha—  
 In order to accelerate the emergence of Gram Sabhas as bodies to 
whom the PRIs are accountable, the powers and functions of Gram 
Sabha should be spelt out in detail articulating their role as planners, 
decision-makers,and auditors. 
 It was agreed that the Gram Sabha meeting should be held at least 
four times in a year. Instead of holding the Gram Sabha on a fixed 
day, it was suggested to hold Gram Sabhas within a span of 30 days 
from the pre-detcrmined dates so that concerned officers are present 
to respond to questions and concerns. 
162 

[1st August 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(v) Transparency and Accountability—  
 It was resolved that the following 4-point strategy for strengthening of Gram  
Sabha and effective  implementation of different  Rural Development 
Schemes will be implemented in letter and spirit:—  
 Awareness through print and electronic media, street plays and training to 
the elected Panchayat representatives; 
 Participation of the community in th e preparation of need based action 
plans, their execution and monitoring; 
 Transparency by displaying all the relevant information on a Bill Board 
regarding estimates, availability of funds and expenditure on the works 
taken, up by the Panchayats, making available all relevant records for 
inspection by the public, providing photocopies of documents, on demand 
on payment of nominal charges and prescribing well-defined methods for 
selection of beneficiaries; 
 Social Audit should have binding legal outcomes so as to curb corruption 
and misutilisation of funds. The Gram Sabha should be empowered 
legally for Social Audit. 
(vi) State Control over PRIs—  
 The scope of State Government intervention and control over 
PRIs should be minimized. If there is any specific complaint 
against any Panchayat, it should be referred to a body similar 
to the Ombudsman in Kerala. 
(vii) Parallel Bodies constituted by States—  
 The Conference decried the increas ing tendency to set up parallel 
bodies. If at all any such bodies arc to be set up, they should work 
under the supervision of the Panchayats and the Gram Sabha. 
 The Conference recommended that instead of setting up parallel 
bodies, States should implement the existing provision in Panchayat 
laws for Sub-Committees on different subjects and train Panchayat 
Members for this purpose. 
 Panchayats/Gram Sabhas should be empowered to supervise and 
monitor the work of NGOs working in the rural areas. 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [1st August 2001] 
(viii) The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled 
Areas) Act 1996-[PESA—1996 ] 
 It was agreed that action would be taken to ensure legislation or 
amendment of relevant Acts/Rules, to bring them in conformity with 
the provisions of the PESA, 1996, latest by 31.3.2002.

employing almost 184 lakh workers arc on the verge of closure due to 
imports from Bangladesh, China and Sri Lanka and excise hike;

(c) the action Government propose to take to make the readymade 
garments sector viable so as to save lakhs of workers engaged in the

† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

[1st August 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
TEXTILES (SHRI V. DHANANJAY KUMAR): (a) to (c) Though the 
import of readymade garments, have shown an increase, the total quantity 
imported is not significant. It is less than even 1% of our domestic garment 
consumption. As regards excise hike, the Government has exempted the 
readymade garment units registered as SSI from the levy of central excise for 
home clearance upto Rs. 1 crore in the case of woven garments. However, 
the import of garments is subject to levy of countervailing duties. 
In order to assist the textile industry including readymade garment industry 
to face international competition, Go vernment has been taking measures 
from time to time. Some of the initiatives taken in this regard are:—  
(1) The Government has imposed a combination of ad-valorem and 
specific duty on "whichever is higher basis" on import of a number of 
textile items to safeguard the interest of domestic industry. 
(2) Government is keeping a watch on the imports and would strive to 
ensure that imports do not cause any serious detriment or injury to the 
domestic industry. In case any unfair trade practices come to the 
notice, action, if necessary, under WTO provisions could be taken. 
(3) A provision of Rs. 10 crores has been earmarked in the Budget 2001-02 
for creating clusters of excellence,  i.e., apparel parks for production 
and export of garments. Besides a provision of Rs. 15 crores has also 
been made for Scheme for improvement of infrastructure facilities at 
major textile production centres. 
(4) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and 
upgradation of this sector so that it can become more competitive in 
international trade. Inter Ministerial Committee to resolve the issues 
pertaining to assistance under TUFS has been constituted.

various courses/programmes to meet skilled manpower 
requirements of textile industry especially apparel in the field of 
design, merchandising and marketing.

facilities by way of eco-testing laboratories.

Constitution of public/private enterprise for tourism development in 
North-East 
1207. SHRI W. ANGOU SINGH: Will the Minister of TOURISM AND 
CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any plan for constituting a public/ private 
enterprise for development of tourism in the North-Eastern Region; 
(b) if so, when will it be constituted; and 
(c) if not, other measures Government propose to take to develop tourism 
in this region? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI ANANTH 
KUMAR): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) Docs not arise. 
(c) As per the PM's initiatives on the North East, the Deptt, of Tourism 
has taken following measures to develop and promote tourism in the North 
Eastern Region. 
 
• 10% of the plan budget of the Department of Tourism has been 
earmarked for development of North East Region. 
• The Department of Tourism has set up a Task Force on the North East 
and the recommendations of the Task  Force are being followed up for 
development of tourism in these areas. 
218 

[1st-August 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
 A chapter of Indian Institute of Tourism and Travel 
Management has recently been opened at Guwahati. 
 A  full  fledged Institute of Hotel  Management  and Catering 
Technology has been set up at Shillong. 
 A video film on tourist attractions for North East has been produced by 
Ministry of Tourism in order to give wide publicity to the region. This is 
being screened by Air India in their flights. 
 North Eastern States arc given a free booth in the World's largest tourism 
fair ITB Berlin. 
 Financial Assistance for promotion of Fairs and Festivals is also being 
provided to North Eastern States every year on continuing basis. 
 North Eastern States arc given a special focus in the Marketing 
Conference of Overseas Offices of the Ministry and all the overseas 
offices arc giving due publicity to the North East States for the promotion 
of tourism in the region. 
 In the first four years of 9th Five Year Plan 340 projects amounting to Rs. 
73.79 crores have been sanctioned and Rs. 27.85 crores have already been 
released to NE States.

permissions to run in shift operations.

(a) whether Government have analys ed the reasons for the economic

(a) Yes, Sir.

terms of gross value added at factor cost) during the years 1999-2000 and 2000-01 
is given in Statement-I (See below). All the sectors, except for 'mining and 
quarrying', have experienced lower growth rate in the year 2000-01 compared to 
that in 1999-2000. The main reasons for the shortfall in the growth performance, 
among others, are the continuing slow growth of agriculture, shortfall in public 
investment and poor governance.

up of agricultural reforms; intensification of infrastructure investment, 
continued reform in the financial sector and capital markets, and deepening of 
structural reforms; human development through better educational opportunities 
and programmes of social security; improvement in the quality of Government 
expenditure; acceleration of disinvestm ent process, etc. Policy initiatives 
announced in the Budget are expected to have a favourable impact on growth during 
the current year. The Planning Commission is in the process of formulating the 
Tenth Five Year Plan to address some of these issues in the medium term 
perspective.

Voluntary Retirement Scheme 
*162. SHRI R.P. GOENKA†          
SHRI BJ. PANDA: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a final view has since has taken on introducing Voluntary 
Retirement Scheme in the Central Government offices; 
(b) if so, the details of the proposals formulated; and 
(c) if not, the present status of considerations of the proposal alongwith the 
details of the difficulties envisaged or of resistance, if any, from within the 
Ministries/Joint Consultative Machinery etc.? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES OF THE 
MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS 
(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Rule 48-A of the Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972 
already provides for Voluntary Retirement Scheme in the Central Government 
Offices. Under this Rule a Government servant can seek voluntary retirement after 
he has completed 20 years of qualifying service by giving notice of not less than 
three months, in writing, to the appointing authority. It further provides that the 
qualifying service as on the date of intended retirement shall be increased by a 
period not exceeding five years subject  to the condition that the total 
qualifying service rendered by the Government servant does not in any case 
exceed 33 years and it does not take him beyond the date of superannuation. 
Rule 29 of the Rules also provides that if a Government servant, on 
being declared surplus to the establishment in which he was serving, opts 
to retire voluntarily, instead of seeking 
†The Question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri R.P. 
Goenka. 
 
18 

[2 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
redeployment, he shall be entitled to have five years added to the 
qualifying service rendered by him subject to the condition that the 
qualifying service rendered by such Government servant is not less than IS 
years on the date on which he exercises such option and the qualifying 
length of service after taking into account the said addition is not more than 
the service he would have rendered had he retired on the date of his 
superannuation. From inception till 30 June, 2001, 9,240 employees 
(belonging to Group A, B&C) were accepted in the Surplus Cell out of 
which 8,771 were redeployed. During this period, 238 persons on rolls of 
the Surplus Cell retired on superannuation or voluntarily. Further 72 
persons were retrenched or resigned during the said period. Thus only 2.7% 
of the persons on the Surplus Cell retired on superannuation or voluntarily. 
The response for voluntary retirement was found to be far from encouraging 
perhaps due to unattractive nature of the existing scheme for surplus 
employees. In view of this, the Expenditure Reforms Commission set up in 
February, 2000 has made the following recommendations in Part II of their 
second Report regarding formulating a revised Voluntary Retirement 
Scheme for surplus personnel: 
(i) Staff declared surplus be transferred to the Surplus Cell to be 
redesignated as the Division of Retraining and Deployment in 
Department of Personnel & Training which will pay their salary, 
retirement benefits etc. However, in such centres, where the number 
of surplus staff is quite small, the present practice of the parent 
organizations making these payments may be continued. 
(ii) Surplus staff should be made eligible for a liberal Voluntary Retirement 
Scheme as recommended by the Fifth Central Pay Commission with 
the exception that commutation entitlements may be as at present and 
the ex-gratia amount may be paid in monthly instalments covering a 
five year period. (The Commission has advised against giving option 
to receive ex-gratia and retirement gratuity in lump sum). 
(iii) In all cases where there is separation by way of liberal 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2001] 
Voluntary   Retirement   Scheme   the   same   order   should stipulate 
the abolition of the resultant vacant post. 
(iv) Group 'A' officials opting for Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) 
should not be required to seek approval for commercial 
employment after retirement. 
(v) Those who do not opt for Voluntary Retirement Scheme and are not 
redeployed within one year should be discharged from service. 
(vi) Redeployment of Group D should be handled by Department of 
Personnel & Training and not Directorate General of Employment & 
Training. 
Action has been initiated by the Government to evolve a revised Voluntary 
Retirement Scheme for the surplus personnel, keeping in view the 
recommendations of the Expenditure Reforms Commission.

*168. SHRI ABANI ROY: 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that Govern ment have recently entered into 
extradition treaties with some of th e foreign countries, if so, the 
details thereof; 
(b) whether any discussions were held before signing the 
extradition treaties with those countries, if so, the details thereof; and 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
50 

[2 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) to what extent the foreign countries have promised to extend help in 
speedy disposal of cases? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): 
(a) Yes, Sir. Extradition Treaties were signed with Federal Republic of 
Germany on 27th June, 2001 and with Republic of Turkey on 29th June, 
2001. The salient features of the Treaties are given in the attached Statement. 
(See below) 
(b) Yes, Sir. India and the Federal Republic of Germany held 
negotiations at official level in 1986 at New Delhi and at Bonn in 
February, 1994. Thereafter, the text was finalized through diplomatic 
channels. Officials of India and Turkey held two rounds of 
negotiations, at Ankara in October, 2000 and at New Delhi in 
December, 2000. Thereafter, th e text was finalized through 
diplomatic channels. 
(c) By signing extradition treaties, the Contracting States provide a 
framework for extradition of fugitive offenders sought by one 
Contracting State from the other. While the Requesting State pursues 
the extradition requests, the actual process often takes time as the 
person sought may attempt to delay the extradition by taking 
recourse to legal avenues availa ble under the domestic laws of the 
Requested State. 
Statement 
Salient features of Extradition Treaty signed with Germany 
(i) Any person who is accused of or convicted for an extraditable 
offence in the Requesting State an d found in the Requested State 
may be extradited to the Requesting State. 
(ii) Any offence punishable with imprisonment or deprivation of liberty 
for a period of one year or more will be an extraditable offence. 
51 

RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2001] 
(iii) Extradition shall not be granted for political offences. The Treaty 
contains a list of offences which wiH not be considered as offences 
of a political character. 
(iv) The Contracting States are not bound to extradite their own nationals, and 
they would be prosecuted by the Requested State in respect of the 
offence(s) in question. 
Salient features of Extradition Treaty signed with Turkey 
(0 The two countries have agreed to extradite any person who, being 
accused or convicted of an extradition offence committed within the 
territory of the one country, is found within the territory of the other 
country. 
(ii) Any offence which is punishable with imprisonment or deprivation of 
liberty for a period of at least one year or by a more severe penalty is 
to be considered as an extraditable offence. 
(iii) A person shall not be extradited if he is a citizen of the Requested 
State or if the offence committed is regarded as a political offence'. The 
Treaty contains a list of offences which will not be considered as 
offences of a political character. 
(iv) Where a request for extradition is refused on the ground of citizenship, the 
Requested State shall submit the case for prosecution to its competent 
authorities provided that the offence for which extradition is sought is 
also an offence under the laws of the Requested State.

(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) and (b) No, Sir. According to the information

Departments were added in the purview of the Directorate. The Directorate is

Change in the Gadgil Formula 
*171. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA:  
         SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are contemplating to change the Gadgil Formula 
regarding the distribution of Central assistance to the States; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) what steps are being taken to ensure  that the States performing well in 
the area of tax mobilization and fis cal management arc not put to a 
disadvantage as a result of the change; 
(d) whether a State's progress on national priorities like population control, 
child care and literacy would be given special incentive; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
PLANNING, STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME 
IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) and (b) Allocation of 
Normal Central Assistance (NCA) for the Annual Plans of States is presently 
based on the Gadgil Formula as approved by the National Development 
Council (NDC) in Decembe r 1991. However, the States have sought a 
revision of this Formula, and accordingly Planning Commission has received 
suggestions from various State Governments. However, there is wide 
divergence in the views amongst the States in this regard. In general, while 
the advanced States have sought higher weightage for performance, the less 
advanced States have sought higher weightage for backwardness. 
63 

 
RAJYA SABHA [2 August, 2001] 
The Full Planning Commission in its meeting held on 27th & 29th June 2001 
discussed, inter-alia, the issue of revision of Gadgil Formula for allocation of 
NCA to States and in view of the, divergence of views among the State 
Governments and the sensitivity of this issue, it was decided that it would be 
necessary to discuss this further and evolve a consensus before alternatives are 
considered by the NDC. 
(c) These aspects, among others, are also taken into consideration 
when the Formula is approved by the NDC. 
(d) The existing formula also give s weightage to indicators of 
performance. These indicators are: Ta x Efforts (2.5%), Fiscal Management 
(2.0%), Population Control (1.0%), Elimination of Illiteracy (1.0%), On-time 
completion of Externally Aided Projects (0.5%) and Land Reforms (0.5%). 
(e) Does not arise.
