Replacement of over-aged rail wagons 
1495. SHRI SURESH PA CHOURI: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the present status of rail wagon industry in the country; 
(b) whether the industry is not getting sufficient orders from the Railways; 
(c) if so, how many rail wagons are overaged today; and 
(d) how Government propose to replace these overaged wagons? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) At presen t, there are 14 wagon manufacturing 
units in the country with wagon build ing capacity of around 40,000 four 
wheeler units. 
(b) Procurement of wagons is dependent upon traffic needs and availability 
of funds. Requirement of wagons in foreseeable future is short of available 
wagon building capacity. As such wagon industry is required to adjust their 
capacities and not to be dependent on Railways alone for utilising their entire 
capacities. 
(c) As on 1.4.2001, there were 26778.5 four wheeler units (FWUs) of 
over-aged BG wagons. 
(d) Over-aged stock is condemned on age-cum-condition basis. 
Replacement of over-aged wagons is done after condemnation 
keeping in view the arising and availability of funds on a year-to-year

Statement-III 
 Rules and Regulations for Occupation of Youth Hostel 
1. Youth Hostel is meant for all tr avellers including YHA Members, 
bona fide students and others connected with YHA movement. It is for the 
inmates to see that the facilities are prop erly utilized and Hostel property is 
not damaged. Any damage to hostel property by them is punishable by the 
Hostel authorities. Right of admission in the Hostel is reserved. 
2. No local person irrespective of his category of YHA membership, 
studentship or any other consideration will be allowed to stay over night in 
the Youth Hostel. 
 
3. Booking in Youth Hostel through Travel Agents is prohibited. 
4. Mostly dormitory type accommodation is provided, separately for 
gents and ladies. The maximum period of stay in the Hostel is three nights, 
which can be extended at the discretion of the Warden, upto seven nights in 
deserving cases. 
5. Prescribed closed hours during day are 1 P.M. to 3 P.M. In exceptional 
circumstances inmates may be permitted to stay during the day. Hostel 
closing time is 11 P.M. 
6. Persons with infectious/contagious di sease are not allowed to stay in 
the hostel. 
7. No person will be allowed to enter the Hostel after closing time at 
night. In exceptional circumstances, inmates may enter after closing time 
with prior permission of the Warden. 
8. Use and/or possession of drugs/alcohol and other intoxicants etc. and 
gambling in the Hostel premises is strictly prohibited. Somking in common 
residential areas is not allowed. 
9. Hostellers should not take visitors to the residential areas. They may, 
however, meet their guests in lounge or other social areas. 
 
10. Hostellers should use their own lock s on the lockers. Hostel does not 
take any responsibility for the loss of their belongings. 
11. Lights off time is 11.30 P.M. 
12. Self-service and performance of any Hostel duty prescribed by 
Warden are normal practices in Youth Hostels.

THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, the recent instances of floods in various parts of the country 
have indeed caused widespread loss of precious lives and property. I share the 
concern of the hon. Members in the matter. 
229 

[RAJYA SABHA] [3 August, 2001] 
Sir, instances of serious floods have occurred from the month of 
June till the end of July in Tripura, Ke rala, Chhattisgarh and most recently in 
Orissa. All these areas have received mo re than their norm al share of rains 
from the South-West monsoon. Thus, while Orissa has received 93 per cent 
more than the last year, such excess in case of Chhattisgarh is 59 per cent, 
Kerala, 33 per cent and Tripura, 70 per cent. Such surplus rain has taken its 
toll. 
Having regard to the extent of area affected in the most recent 
floods, Orissa should be referred at the very outset. People of the State who 
had undergone serious trauma in the super cyclone of October, 1999 and had, 
subsequently, suffered drought, were again at the receiving end of the nature's 
fury. Floods in Orissa occurred in three phases. The first was in the beginning 
of July, 2001, caused by heavy rains in the catchment area of Mahanadi and 
the release of water from certain reservoirs in Chhattisgarh into the Mahanadi 
system. This resulted in inundation in large number of districts, including 
Puri, Jagatsinghpur, Bhadrak, Khurda, Kedrapara and Kalahandi etc. With the 
abatement of-rains, the water receded around nm July. 
Again, following recurrence of torrential rains, sluice-gates of the 
overflowing Hirakud reservoir had to be opened. The resultant outflow with 
other run-off caused by the next round of extensive rains caused serious 
floods in 24 districts. The situation aggravated due to high tide which slowed 
down drainage in the Bay of Bengal. The situation eased by about 22 nd July, 
only to recur around 25 th July, 2001, with the next round of rains which 
affected many districts, again, includ ing Jagatsinghpur, Bhadrak, Kedrapara 
and parts of Puri. In all, 96 human lives were lost, with more than 16,201 
villages and 80 lakh persons being aff ected; 8.75 lakh hectares of cropped 
area and 2,05,760 houses had also been affected. The State Government rose 
to the occasion and deployed all ava ilable resources for relief and rescue, 
which resulted in a much lesser toll of life than was possible, given the 
magnitude of the flood. Six lakh people were evacuated to safer places, and 
relief materials, along with medicines, were sent to the affected areas. The 
losses are yet to be assessed and quantified, in detail, as the State Government 
machinery is rightly concentrating on providing immediate relief. 
The Central Government has been in constant touch with the State 
Government, providing all possible assistance from the very first phase. The 
situation was reviewed by the National Crisis Management Committee, under 
230 

 
[3 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
the chairmanship of the Cabinet Secretary, on 18 th July, 2001, and necessary 
directions were issued to various agencies of the Central Government to 
extend the required assistance to the State Governments and for restoration of 
the damaged infrastructure. As always , the Armed Forces played a very 
useful role in relief and rescue operations with the deployment of 8 army 
columns, helicopeters and aircraft of IAF and provision of medical care, etc. 
Railways, which suffered extensive damage in the State have not only 
managed to restore most of the damage (except a bridge near Jharsuguda), 
have been transporting relief materials and supplies free of cost; 2,400 tents 
have been made available free of cost. The Ministry of Health, apart from 
sending a team, have rushed necessary supplies. At the instance of the Prime 
Minister, Shri Nitish Kumar, my predecessor, made an on-the-spot 
assessment of 19 th July, along with the hon. Central Ministers from Orissa, 
the Cabinet Secretary, the Secretary (A griculture & Cooperation) and other 
senior offices, and reviewed the relief measures. 
The Prime Minister also visited the State on 29th July and announced 
a number of measures to provide im mediate and long-term relief to the 
affected people. This includes release of Rs.100 crores as an ad hoc assistance 
from the National Calamity Contingency Fund, release of 3 lakh tonnes of 
rice for the Food for Work Programme, which will cost around Rs.210 crores, 
and construction of one lakh housing units for people living below the 
poverty line, under the Indira Aawas Yojana, which will cost about Rs.225 
crores. Once the extent of damage is  fully assessed, a Central Team, which 
has been constituted, will be sent to the State to determine the extent of 
assistance required from the National Calamity Contingency Fund. 
The floods in Kerala which were preceded by landslides around 7 th 
July took a heavy toll of more than hundred human lives. The total damage in 
monetary terms projected by the State Government is Rs.551.75 crores. The 
first instalment of 50 per cent of the Central share of the Calamity Relief 
Fund (CRF) of Rs.26.48 crores has already been released, and the Ministry of 
Finance is requested to also release the second instalment, in advance. A 
Central Team has just returned from th e State after assessing the situation, 
and the allocation to be made from the NCCF to the State will soon be 
decided. Like Orissa, the Army, the Navy and the Coast Guard rendered the 
most useful assistance to the State Government. My predecessor reviewed the 
position at Thiruvananthapuram on 14th July for an on-the-spot assessment. 
231 

[RAJYA SABHA] [3 August, 2001] 
Chhattisgarh too suffered floods from 9 July which affected 
Dhamtari district and other catchment areas of the Mahanadi system affecting 
23 tehsils and resulting in a loss of 12 lives. The State Government has 
projected a loss of Rs. 102 crores. It has been decided to depute a Central 
team to the State. Further assistance from NCCF will be considered in the 
light of the report of the team. 
Earlier, Tripura and the adjoining districts of Assam and Meghalaya 
suffered flash floods, which mainly caused damage to the national highway 
connecting the State to the rest of the country. The Border Roads 
Organisation and the Army took up restoration work on a war-footing basis 
and opened the highway in a record time of 6 days. No memorandum for 
further assistance has been received from these States. 
While primarily it is the responsibility of the respective State 
Governments to deal with the natural calamities including floods, the Central 
Government is committed to supplementing their efforts by making available 
all possible logistic and financial support. The Department of Agriculture and 
Cooperation has been closely monitoring the situation in all the States and is 
in constant touch with the affected States. A Control Room is functioning for 
the purpose round the clock and situation reports are being issued regularly. 
The details are also available on the website of the Natural Disaster 
Management Division of the Department. Developments requiring prompt 
attention are being constantly reviewed at  the level of the Department as also 
the Cabinet Secretary in the National Crisis Management Committee. I take 
this opportunity to assure this House that we will not be wanting in 
responding to any call for assistance from  the States to mitigate the suffering 
and hardship of the people affected by floods.

SHRI N. K. PREMACHANDRAN (K erala): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I 
would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Agriculture to the 
havoc caused by floods throughout th e country. While some States like 
Kerala, Orissa and so on are having fl oods, there are other States which are 
facing the drought situation. Those are the conditions prevailing in our 
country. Effective management of thes e calamities is not being done, even 
after fifty years of our independence. 
As far as floods are concerned, par ticularly in my State of Kerala, 
we have been having floods to such an extent that we have never experienced 
in the last ten to fifteen years. As it has been mentioned in the statement made 
by the hon. Minister, more than 107 people have died because of the havoc 
caused by floods. It has already been mentioned in the House that about 
20,000 families were rendered homeless in Kerala and about 35,000 families 
had to be evacuated to the relief camps. The damage caused to agricultural 
crops and roads alone amounts to Rs.407 crores. Last week, a team of experts 
visited most of the parts of Kerala. I am sure they must have been convinced 
that the damage caused to the agricu ltural produce, the damage caused to 
roads and the damage caused to the houses in most of the parts of Kerala, has 
been huge. I hope the team of experts has submitted its report also. 
My submission is, as compared to  other States, there is another 
phenomena so far as my State of Kerala is concerned. Kerala's seashore is 
about 560 kms., that is, from Parassala to Kasaragod, from south to north. 
The whole coastal area has been damage d. It is a heavy damage caused to 
roads. The fishermen have been affected badly and the whole industrial belt 
has also been affected badly. And this is not due to the west monsoon alone. 
The sea erosion is a phenomenon that is being experienced every year. Out of 
these 560 kms. of coastal area, we have already built seawalls in about 480 
kms. with the assistance from the Central Government. But what has 
happened to these sea walls? Up to 1991-92, that is, up to the 7 m Plan, we 
were getting Central Assistance for construction and maintenance of these  sea-
walls and there was a  Ran  allocation  for the  purpose.

But after the 7 th Plan, the allocation has been nil. No Central 
Assistance is being given to Kerala, so far as the protection of sea-shore is 
concerned. And this is the situation not only in the case of Kerala, but also in 
the case of all the other maritime States. So, through this Calling Attention 
motion, I would like to request the hon. Minister that sufficient Central 
assistance as Plan allocation has to be gi ven to the maritime States so as to 
enable them to protect their sea-shor es, the coastal areas. As I mentioned 
earlier, Kerala has a coastal area of 56 0 kms. and immediately to the east of 
it, there are backwaters and we have the National Waterways. The distance 
between the National Waterways or the backwaters and the sea is just below 
100 meters. It is a sort of a strip of land. There is always a danger of any 
havoc taking place there. It is also a 1 very heavily populated area.  The 
coastal area is a highly populated area. 
We can divide the whole State into midlands, highlands and the 
coastal area. As far as the coastal area is concerned, it is thickly populated. 
We have the fish processing industry, the mineral industries, and also the coir 
industry concentrated in the coastal ar ea. These have been totally damaged. 
The sea-walls have been damaged. Since there has been no maintenance, the 
walls have already collapsed. As far as the midlands are concerned, a major 
damage has been caused to agriculture. There are land slides in the highlands 
of Kerala, especially in Idukki and such other places. It  was reported in 
almost all the newspapers and other media that an eminent photographer, Mr. 
Victor George, died on the spot while he was filming, the landslides. It was 
the worst tragedy that o ccurred in our State. He was filming the damage 
caused by landslides. A total of 107 persons, including Mr. Victor George, 
died. The overall loss caused because of damage of agriculture, houses, sea-
shores, midlands and so on in Kerala has been assessed to be of the order of 
Rs.600 crores. It is pathetic. I ask very humbly. What has been the assistance 
provided by the Government of India. In my opinion, nothing has been done 
till now. I am not blaming the Government. Sufficient relief should be 
provided to all the States. As Shri Suresh Pachouri mentioned, there should 
be no discrimination In giving relief in flood and other such situations. I feel 
there has been discrimination. I fully support whatever relief has already been 
given to Orissa and it may not have been sufficient also. I appreciate that an 
amount of Rs.100 crores was first announced by the hon. Prime Minister. 
Subsequently, immediately after the aerial survey during his visit, he again

words, I conclude. 
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN (Kerala): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, thank 
you for allowing me to speak on this Motion. 
Sir, natural calamities like flood, dr ought, cyclone and sea-erosion are 
taking place every year in the Southern St ates. Our country is so big that when 
there are devastating floods in some St ates, some States suffer from severe 
drought. These calamities result in deaths of hundreds of people. Thousands 
and thousands of houses are squarely damaged or they are washed away. 
Agricultural crops are being damaged on a very large scale. Even perennial 
crops like coconut, rubber and coffee are being destroyed. Lakhs of families 
have lost all that they have, and they have become destitutes; they have been 
left with no clothes, food and shelter. Agricultural workers, poor and middle 
level peasants and the rural poor are the people who have been hit very hard. 
When such calamities take place, relief measures will have to be organised on a 
very large scale. The State Governments will not be having the resources to 
fulfil this responsibility. Therefore, the Ce ntre will have to give assistance to 
the States. Of course, the Centre is granting financial assistance to several 
States.   But there is a. -

feeling that discrimination is shown to some States which are ruled by parties 
or combination of parties not belonging to the ruling front. In West Bengal, 
for instance, last year, a very severe, devastating flood, occurred, affecting 
nearly eight districts. The Chief Minist er and the various Ministers of West 
Bengal and also the Members of Parliament belonging to West Bengal came 
to Delhi; they sat on a dharna demanding help from the Centre. But no 
assistance was given. Now, in Kerala, an unprecedented flood situation has 
taken place, and no assistance has so fa r been given. I am not against giving 
assistance to the States ruled by the c onstituents of the NDA. Of course, if 
necessary, they may be given more assistance. We are not against that. But, at 
the same time, there should be an equa l treatment to everybody; there should 
be no discrimination. Sir, it is a matter of shame that the Central Government, 
in cooperation with the State Governments, have not so far set up a permanent 
machinery to carry on the relief work. In the matter of flood control, the first 
thing that needs to be done is strengthening of the bunds on the banks of the 
river. For decades together, much is being said about the linkage of the 
various big rivers. If that was done, floods could have been controlled to a 
great extent. The available water could have been utilised in extending the 
irrigation facilities and also for providing safe drinking water. At least now, 
the Government should see to it that the relief work is taken up. Until then, 
the accumulated grain stocks with the Go vernment could be made available. 
With these words, I conclude. Thank you, Sir.

received heavy rainfall during the Sout h-West monsoon resulting in floods, 
landslides, loss of human life and cattle, destruction of houses, disruption of 
communication networks and so on; a lot of inconveniences have been caused 
to the people because of this heavy loss. 
It was reported that during the period from June 1 to July 11, 2001, 
28 out of 35 meteorological subdivisions covering 75 per cent districts and 85

period. The overall situation is that th e country as a whole received 19 per

regarding the calamities on account of these floods, I do not intend to go into 
the details of that. I would only confine myself to the calamities that have 
struck my State during this South-West monsoon. The South-West monsoon 
started in Kerala on 25.5.2001. There was severe sea erosion in all   the

SHRI RANGANATH MISRA (Orissa): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I 
am happy that an opportunity has been given to me to speak on the floods in 
Orissa. I will take just ten minutes and finish my speech. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI RAMA SHANKER KAUSHIK): 
No. Please take only five minutes. 
SHRI RANGANATH MISRA: I will try. The last four years have 
been very unfortunate for the State of Orissa. I have been told that 1998 had a 
very hot season; and about 4,000 people died. Then, next the super-cyclone 
came. Then, came a total drought in the entire State. This year it has been 
affected by floods, which is very unusual. In a sense, we got three rounds of 
low pressure. Each one was concentrat ed in the catchment area of all our 
rivers. On account of that, the water le vel had gone up; and most of the areas 
have been badly affected. It is very difficult to assess the extent of human 
suffering. By the time a Central team will go and assess the damage and then 
decide the compensation, it will be too late, However, compensation is not 
going to take away the sufferings of the flood-affected people. Already, they 
are undergoing great suffering. Usually,' the compensation announced by the 
Government is not adequate. I was surpri sed when the Minister indicated that 
the extent of loss has not yet been worked out. If it is not worked out in time, 
then, you will not be in a position to  compensate the people appropriately 
because, later on, the evaluation would be defective. 
I went to some areas which have  been affected by the floods, 
particularly, areas close to my town. I found that the daily necessities are not 
being supplied. Kerosene is not available. Lighting facility is not being 
provided. Medical treatment is not being provided. Transport by boat is not 
249 

[RAJYA SABHA] [3 August, 2001] 
available. Some of the boatmen have been charging more because of  more 
demand and less supply. 
The other thing is, when the super- cyclone came two years back, we 
talked of a permanent arrangement so th at the State did not suffer. Orissa, by 
its geographical location is exposed to these types of natural calamities. It is a 
special State, by location. Unless you find a permanent solution, providing 
compensation every year is no solution.  Three years ago, when we were 
discussing about permanent measures, we thought that something would 
emerge. But, as time rolled by, the Government forgot it completely. So far, 
nothing has been done. In view of the sufferings of the people, we must do 
something for them, on a permanent basis, instead of providing compensation 
every year. For that purpos e, there has been a demand from all of us. I hope 
Government will understand its responsibility. Orissa has been rated as one of 
the poorest States of the country. Therefore, a poor  State to come up to the 
national level, requires special assistance. I would suggest to the Government 
of India that in addition to providing compensation for the loss that it has 
suffered recently, they should provide special protection to the State, provide 
generous financial assistance so that th e State can come out of its  present 
predicament. 
The difficulties that we have been facing for a long time require a 
permanent solution. Let us not forget that the demand of Orissa has to be met, 
on a permanent basis. I appeal, through you, Sir, to the Central Government 
for extending generous financial support ,to us to tackle this situation 
scientifically with appropriate engineerin g tactics. What is required is collate 
it together so that this type of natural calamity does not recur. This annual 
event is breaking the economy of the St ate. Poverty is increasing because, 
every year, a chunk of the State is ge tting affected. Whatever area is being 
rehabilitated again, it is affected again due to natural calamity. That is why, in 
these 50 years of independence, Ori ssa has not been able to make any 
progress and come to the mainstream. Therefore, all of us demand for finding 
a permanent solution to this problem. I hope this message would be conveyed 
to the Central Government for appropriate handling. 
The overall picture of the situa tion shows that the common man is 
not able to come up. If the Government is interested in the total development 
of all the States, then, I suggest that Orissa should be extended a special 
benefit facility and generous assistance for this year. A permanent financial 
assistance be provided to the State of Orissa in future

also so that the State is able to come up and compete with the other States.

PRIVATE MEMBER'S RESOLUTION 
Increasing erosion of federal principles in Centre-State relations due to the 
Union Government usurping the powers of the State Governments 
SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI (Kerala): Sir, I beg to move 
the 
following resolution: 
"That this House expresses its deep concern over the increasing 
erosion of the federal principles in Centre-State relations due to 
the Union Government usurping the powers of the State 
Governments." 
Sir, I move this resolution to bring to the notice of this august House 
this important subject of Centre-State relations and also to bring to the notice 
of this House the growing erosion of th e powers of the States because of the 
commissions and omissions on the part of the Central Government. 
Sir, this issue of Centre-State relations is intimately and inherently 
connected with the issue of unity and integrity of the country. Sir, our country 
is a heterogeneous land of diverse languages, culture, ethnicity and history. If 
we look at the whole history of India, we can find periods of unity and 
stability and also we can see periods of dissensions, chaos and fragmentation. 
Sir, there were many attempts in the past for over-centralisation, but all those 
attempts proved counter-productive. On the other hand, these attempts were 
met by a chain reaction from the divisive fo rces. It is also a fact. If we look at 
the whole history of India, our province s and our local bodies enjoyed, in the 
past, autonomy and more powers. The whole history from the Mauryas to the 
Mughals was a proof of this. Sir, when the Britishers came to India, when they 
started establishing their power in India, they tried to concentrate all powers at 
the Centre. All those attempts were resisted by the people; and they were 
forced to give more autonomy and powers to the States. 
Sir, after Independence, in 1950, the Constitution came into 
existence. Its provisions elaborately d eal with the issue of Centre-State 
relations. I am not going into those pr ovisions. We have, on many occasions, 
discussed about those provisions. The essence of Centre-State relations is 
brought out by the report on Centre-State relations, in a brief manner. I would 
like to quote a paragraph from the report on Centre-State 
262 

[3 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
relations. This report is commonly called the Sarkaria Commission Report. 
Page 9, paragraph 1.3.04 deals with this particular aspect: 
"The Constitution, as it emerges from the Constituent Assembly in 
1949, has important federal features. But it can't be called federal in 
the classical sense. It can't be ca lled unitary either. It envisages a 
diversified political system of special type. According to Dr. B.R. 
Ambedkar, Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent 
Assembly, it is unitary in extraordinary situations, such as war or 
emergency, and, federal in normal times. Some authorities have 
classified it as a quasi-federal Constitution. However, these labels 
hardly matter, as both levels of Governments derive respective 
powers from a written Constitution, which is supreme and there is a 
Supreme Court to interpret the Constitution. " 
So what do we derive from this? One of the important elements of 
the Constitution is its federal nature. It is also a fact that the Constitution 
contains elements of Central domina tion over the States. Sir, I consider 
federalism or multi-level governance as  the best founding principle of 
politics. It has two main advantages. One, each individual unit derives 
strength from the unity; on the other hand, each individual unit can retain its 
autonomy and specific identity. So, it is a blend of these two qualities. 
Sir, for building better Centre-State relations, the Union and the 
State should work in tandem, for the common welfare, on the basis of 
cooperative federalism. We should also try to strengthen the institutions and 
conventions. Sir, instead of strengthening the federal principles, there is a 
growing trend on the part of the Central Government is concentrating more 
and more powers at the Centre, usurping the rights and powers of the States. 
Sir, this trend is dangerous to the un ity and integrity of our country. This 
trend is dangerous for good governance of our country. This particular aspect 
is very picturesquely and vividly dealt with in the Sarkaria Commission 
Report. I would like to read that particular part about the growing trend of 
over-centralisation in India. 
On page 534, paragraph 21.2.07, it is stated: 
"Since for reasons explained elsewhere in this Report, there is a 
general tendency towards greater cen tralisation of powers, there is 
special need in a country like In dia for a conscious and purposive 
effort to counter it all the time. There is considerable truth in the 
263 

[RAJYA SABHA] [3 August, 2001] 
saying that undue centralisation leads to blood pressure at the Centre 
and anaemia at the peri phery. The inevitable result is morbidity and 
inefficiency. Indeed, centralisation does not solve bu t aggravate the 
problems of the people. " 
Sir, this is what the Report on Centre-State Relations States about 
over-centralisation. This is what is really happening in our country and 
because of the over-centralisation, th e fissiparous tendencies are gaining 
strength and the divisive forces ar e making use of it. Even the foreign 
hand gets an opportunity to intervene and make use of the present situation 
for their fissiparous aims. You transfer  more powers to the States. Now, 
after 73 rd Amendment of the Constitution, the Panchayati Raj Institutions 
have come into existence. We have to devolve more powers to the States 
and the States should also give more powers to the Panchyati Raj 
institutions. It does not mean that we stand for a weaker Centre and we 
stand for stronger States. No, not at all. We-stand for a strong Centre, 
strong   States  and   also  strong   Panchayati   Raj   Institutions.  In   this 
connection, I would like to bring to the notice of this august House a note 
prepared by the Communist Party of India (Marxist) for the conclave of the 
opposition parties which was held in Sri Nagar on October 5-7, 1983. I would 
like to quote one paragraph from that proposal of the Communist Party of 
India (Marxist) on the question of Centre-State relations. It says, "We stand 
for the unity of the country and fight all forces of disintegration. We definitely 
stand for an effective and efficient Ce ntre capable of defending the country, 
organising and consolidating its economic life and adequately armed with 
powers to discharge its other jobs like foreign policy, communication, foreign 
trade, etc." 
So there is no doubt about it. We stand for a stronger Centre. We 
also stand for stronger States and stronger Panchayati Raj institutions. That 
can find solution to the problems, that can bring the unity of the people and 
that alone can keep the integrity of the country in this complex international 
situation. Sir, instead of strengthening the Centre and the States, the attitude 
of the Central Government through its commissions and omissions is of 
weakening both the Centre and the Stat es. We can see two trends; on the one 
hand, the Centre is trying to usurp, encroach upon the rights of the States and, 
on the other hand, the Centre is abdicating its responsibilities. That leads to a 
situation where fissiparous tendencies can gain strength and do harm to the 
unity and integrity of the country. Sir, firstly, I would like to deal with the 
aspect of over-centralisation on the part 
264 

[3 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
of the Central Government. One of the most important issues is with regard to 
the division of fiscal powers. There is a consistent complaint on the part of 
the States that the division of powers on fiscal matters is balanced more in 
favour of the Centre than the States. The States have only limited fiscal power 
as compared to the powers of the Centre. 
Most of the States are critical ab out these things and most of the 
States are asking for more and more pow ers the transfer of tax revenue, the 
institution of Finance Commission, the institution of Planning Commission, 
their sphere of activities, their decisions on the transfer of tax revenue and 
their decision on giving grants and loan s. We can find that there is an over-
centralisation of powers at the Cent re. It is a basic structure of the 
Constitution i.e., devolution of powers on this matter. Now, the Union 
Government is trying to encroach upon the limited powers that the States 
have, according to the present Cons titution. The Central Government 
constituted the Eleventh Finance Commission, but, subsequently, made a 
change in the terms of reference, as additional terms of reference. The 
intention of the Central Government was to get a recommendation from the 
Finance Commission so that the Central Government can monitor the fiscal 
policies of the States. So, they made that change in the terms of reference and 
the Eleventh Finance Commission submitted its Additional Report. In that 
Report, it had recommended monitoring of the fiscal policies of the States, 
making use of the instrumentality of statutory financial devolution. This is a 
serious encroachment on the. rights of the States in formulating their fiscal 
policies and instruments. There is another aspect to it. This matter was 
considered in the Inter-State Council, constituted as per the provisions of the 
Constitution. This matter was, specifically, discussed on May 20, 2000, in the 
Inter-State Council meeting. Many State Governments, raised objection on 
this; at that time, the Additional Report of the Eleventh Finance Commission 
was not submitted. Then, the hon. Finance Minister assured the Inter-State 
Council that the Government would come back to the Inter-State Council with 
the recommendations of the Eleventh Finance Commission and a decision 
would be taken only after consultation. But, Sir, subsequently, there was no 
consultation at all. The Central Government, unilaterally, took a decision. 
Certainly, this is an encroachment on the rights of the States. 
There is another threat. That is also coming in slowly. This is an 
encroachment, coming through the Finance Commission. Now, the Central 
Government is trying to encroach upon the rights of the States through the 
265 

[RAJYA SABHA] [3 August, 2001] 
instrument of the Planning Commission. Recently, the hon. Prime Minister's 
Economic Advisory Committee submitted a Report called, "Economic 
Reforms and Mid-term Appraisal." Th ere, in that Report, there is a 
recommendation that from the Tenth Plan onwards, i.e., starting from 1 st 
April, 2002, half of the normal Cent ral assistance to State Plans should be 
provided only on the basis of assessment of the fiscal reform plan formulated 
by the Centre. 
So, through these two institutions-the Finance Commission and the 
Planning Commission-the Centre is trying to usurp the limited rights of the 
States, with regard to fiscal matters.  This is a very serious matter.

OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN. Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the 
Ming away of Begum Aizaz Rasul, a former Member of this House on 
the August, 2001, at the age of 93 after a prolonged illness at Lucknow. 
lorn at Lahore in April, 1909 Begam Aizaz Rasul had her education at Went 
of Jesus and Mary, Shimla and at Queen Mary's College, Lahore. An active 
social and political worker, Begam Aizaz Rasul was associated with various 
educational and social welfare organisations in different capacities. 
The distinguished Legislative career of Begam Aizaz Rasul started with 
the memberships of U.P. Legislative Council of which she was a member from 
1937 to 1952. She held the office of the Deputy President of the U.P. Legislative 
Council from 1937 to 1940. She also act ed as the Leader of the Opposition, 
U.P. Legislative Council from 1950 to 1952. 
Later, Begam Aizaz Rasul was a Member of the Constituent Assembly of India 
mar 1946 to 1950. She represented the State of Uttar Pradesh in this House from 
April 1952 to April 1956. Thereafter, she was elected as a Member of the U.P. 
gislative Council in 1957 and remained there till 1968 and she got elected to 
P. Legislative Assembly in 1969. She was again elected to that Assembly in 
1977, 1980 and 1985. She also served as a Minister in the Government of Uttar 
Pradesh holding the portfolio of Social Welfare from 1969 to 1971. 
In the passing away of Begam Aizaz Rasul, the country has lost a veteran 
parliamentarian, a distinguished social worker and a champion of the causes 
of women. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Begam Aizaz Rasul. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of 
respect to the memory of the departed. 
(The hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.)

Import of Medicines 
*201. SHRI P. K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that import of medicines of doubtful 
quality is taking place through some unknow sources in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the reasons for dumping these medicines into the country; 
(d) whether Government propose to amend the Drgus and Cosmetics Act; 
and 
(e) if not, the other measures to be taken by Government to check such 
imports? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.R 
THAKUR): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Tabic of the House. 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [6 August, 2001 ] 
Statement 
(a) to (e) No Sir, there is not report of dumping of doubtful quality drugs in 
the country by unknown sources. 
Imported drugs for domestic consumption are required to comply with all 
the provisions as prescribed in the Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules 
made thereunder. Accordingly, Custom s Authorities forward the bill of entry 
or any application in this regard to the port officers of the CDSCO offices at 
ports and airports for scrutiny prior to  clearance for import. These documents 
mandatorily include the name and address of the importer, name and quantity 
of the drugs, and the name and address of the manufacturer/supplier. 
All the documents related to every import consignment of drugs is examined 
by the Port Officers. Samples are draw n at random for testing at Government 
or Government approved laboratories to  ensure that these products comply 
with domestic quality requirements. Further, every batch of imported vaccines 
is tested at Central Research Institute , Kasauli, and every batch of imported 
blood products is tested at identified labs. Drugs which do not meet the required 
quality parameters are not cleared for marketing in the country. 
While existing provisions in the Drugs & Cosmetics Act and Rules 
thereunder ensure that drugs of doubt ful quality are not imported into the 
country, these provisions are being further strengthened by introducing a 
Registration System for foreign manufacturers and their products, prior to such 
products being allowed for import into the country. The draft rules in this 
regard have been notified and they are being finally published shortly. 
SHRI P. K. MAHESHWARI: Sir, the markets of North-India are flooded 
with spurious and illegally imported, smuggled, medicines, especially from 
China. These drugs do not come under any label or brand, but are being openly 
sold in the chemists' shops. My first supplementary to the hon. Minister is : 
Will he ensure that these substandard and cheaper drugs do not get into the 
Government programmes and hospitals so that the people from the weaker 
sections, who avail of this facility, are not put to any inconvenience of getting 
such type of drugs for their treatment? 
DR. C. P. THAKUR: Sir, actually, the hon. Member has raised three issues 
in his supplementary. The first one is: Spurious drugs are imported from China. 
The second one is, those spurious drugs are illegally imported; and the third 
one is, we should ensure that these drugs do not enter into the health programmes 
of the Government and the people do not suffer. Sir, spurious drugs have not

The Department of Commerce has taken action against this dumping. We 
are checking the substandard drugs at the ports. If there are such drugs, they 
have to inform to the drug control o fficers who are there. There are some 
laboratories which check the quality of the drugs. If they are found substandard, 
they are returned or destroyed. That we do. So far as the industry is concerned, 
actually, the industry has mostly been vociferous about the fake drugs 
manufactured in this country. What th ey do is, they manufacture two- three 
types of fake drugs. First, they just copy the brand name of some of the leading 
pharmaceutical companies. Secondly, the drugs may be good, but the 
pharmaceutical companies, which really manufacture those drugs, suffer because 
in the market, their drugs have to compete with the drugs made by the fake 
companies. Thirdly, the drugs are sometimes substandard. Say, instead of 250

mg. of drug in a particular capsule, they put only 200 mg. of drug. Fourthly, 
there may not be any drug at all. So, recently, raids were conducted in different parts 
of Delhi, at places like Bhagirath Place. Some such companies were found there. 
Cases have been instituted. We have alerted all the State Governments because it is 
a State subject. We had a meeting of alt the Drug Controllers of different States. 
They have to work in tandem with the police of that State. They have to detect those 
drugs by deploying inspectors, etc. Then, they have to be tested. So, we are

look into this matter. Our Ministry is the user Ministry. Trie Ministry of Chemicals

Ministry of Commerce is the nodal Ministry to look into the dumping. Fourthly, the 
Ministry of Finance is the regulatory Ministry. So, we will take a very 
comprehensive view of it.

Market borrowings of SAIL  
203. SHRI B. J. PANDA: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) the level of total market borrowing of SAIL as on 30th June, 2001; 
(b) how much, out of that, is high cost debt (interest between 15—17 
per cent); 
(c) the action plan to refinance this high cost debt; and 
(d) how much low cost borrowing (interest 10—12 per cent) was made in 
the year 2000-2001 and how much high cost debt was repaid out of this? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OFTHE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI BRAJ 
KISHORE TRIPATHY): (a) to (d) A stat ement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
12 

[6 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
(a) The level of total market borrowing of Steel Authority of India Limited 
(SAIL) as on 30th June, 2001 is Rs. 14101 crores. 
(b) Out of that, Rs. 960 crores is high cost debt (interest rate between 
15—17 per cent). 
(c) The entire amount of Rs. 960 crores is due for maturity during the current 
financial year. This is proposed to be repaid out of market borrowing, the proceeds 
of assets restructuring and reduction in working capital. 
(d) SAIL made borrowings of Rs. 1287 crores, comprising of Bonds, Term 
Loans etc. which include Rs. 347 crore of  loans bearing interest at less than 
12% per annum. The balance amount of Rs. 940 crore was raised at interest 
rate between 12% to 13.05% per annum. Rs. 923 crores were utilised for 
repayment of high cost Bonds (interest rate between 15—17 per cent). 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: Sir, in the statement laid by the hon. Minister, it has 
been indicated that less than seven per cent of the debt of the Steel Authority of 
India is high cost debt, and also that the entire portion of the high cost debt is 
due for maturity and repayment during this year. It also indicates that the pain 
for repaying the debt is based on some borrowings at lower costs this year as 
well as restructuring of assets. If I may refer to the restructuring plan of SAIL, 
approved by the Government of India last year, one of the major areas that it 
focuses on is the management principle of concerntrating on core competence. 
In other words, the plan indicates that a steel maker should get out of those 
operations which do not have much to do with steel. In particular, it mentions 
disposal of non- core assets such as pow er plants, oxygen plants etc. I would 
like to seek a clarification from the Minister whether this is being implemented, 
and, to what extent, these non-core assets are being disposed of to take care of 
the financial restructuring. 
SHRI BRAJ KISHORE TRIPATHY: Sir, so far the proposal concerning the 
repayment of high cost debts is concerned, the entire amount is proposed to be 
repaid out of market borrowings, the proceeds of assets restructuring and by 
reducing the working capital. There are so many proposals. Business 
restructuring is not the only proposal through which the repayment of debt 
will be made. So far as the business restructuring is concerned, the proposal is 
going on smoothly. The proposal concerning divestment of the non-core assets, 
so far as the power plant is concerned, has also been going on smoothly since 
last year. And, this year also, there is also proposal for business restructuring.

SHRI BRAJ KISHORE TRIPATHY: Sir, we are also touching the world 
market. There is a good improvement, so far as exports are concerned. Last 
year, we had exported 3MT tonnes of our steel products. Presently, the market 
is sluggish in our country, and internationally also, the condition is not good 
for the steel sector. The developing countries are taking protective measures to 
discourage imports into their countries. Despite that, we are taking all steps 
and we are finding out how to increase our exports. It is true that the domestic 
consumption of steel is much less in comparision to many other parts of the 
world. To give you an example, the per capita consumption of steel in our 
country is only 26 kg., whereas it is 90 kg. in China; it is more than 400 kg., in 
the U.S.A. and more than 600 kg. in Japan. So, we are interested in seeing that 
the domestic consumption of steel increases so that whatever we produce has a 
market in our own country.

* 212. MIRZA ABDUL RASHID: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state:

urban areas/cities of J and K State;

THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION (SHRI JAGMOHAN): (a) The details of the Centrally-
sponsored schemes being implemented by Ministry of Urban Development 
and Poverty Alleviation for development of urban areas/cities in J and K 
State are as under: 
(1) INTEGRATED DEVELOPMENT OF SMALL AND MEDIUM 
TOWNS (IDSMT): The objective of the scheme is to improve infrastructural 
facilities and helping in the creation of durable public assets in small and 
medium towns. The Scheme is applicable to cities having a population upto 5 
lakhs. 
(2) LOW COST SANITATION SCHEME FOR LIBERATION OF 
SCAVENGERS: It provides for conversion of existing dry latrines into low 
cost water seal pour flush latrines and construction of new sanitary units 
where none exist, to prevent open defecation. The basic objective is to liberate 
the scavengers from the obnoxious practice of carrying head loads of nightsoil 
and the scheme is being implemented on a whole town basis. 
(3) ACCELERATED URBAN WATER SUPPLY PROGRAMME 
(AUWSP): The scheme was initiated with the objective of solving the drinking 
water problems in towns having population less than 20,000 as per 1991 census. 
Considering the water scarcity and the narrow revenue base of these small 
towns, the scheme is funded by the Central and State Governments in the ratio 
of 50:50. 
(4) SWARNA JAYANTI SHAHARI ROZGAR YOJANA (SJSRY): The 
Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rojgar Yojana  (SJSRY) Seeks to provide gainful 
employment to the urban unemployed or underemployed through encouraging 
die setting up of self-employment ventures or provision of wage employment. 
This programme relies on creation of suitable community structures and delivery 
of inputs is through the medium of urban local bodies and such community 
structure. The SJSRY is funded on a 75:25 basis between Centre and the States.

Karnataka, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Manipur and Nagaland to review the

*219. SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there are some differences between the Ministry 
of Social Justice and Empowerment and Maharashtra Food and Drug 
Administration regarding anti-snake venom serum being produced by State-
run Haffkin Bio-Pharmaceutical Company; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) whether the differences have been settled and the production of serum 
resumed as per the Central advice? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) Haffkine Bio- Pharmaceutical Corporation Limited 
(HBPCL), Mumbai, is a public sector undertaking under the Government of 
Maharashtra, engaged in manufacture of various biological and non-biological 
drugs, vaccines and sera, including Anti Snake Venom Serum (ASVS). After 
the "Breeding of and Experiments on Animals (Control & Supervision) Rules, 
1998" under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, came into force, 
it has become necessary for HBPCL to register itself with the Committee for 
the purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CPCSEA). 
HBPCL got itself registered with the CPCSEA under Rule 5-A of the Breeding 
of and Experiments on Animals (Control & Supervision) Rule, 1998 in June, 
2000. This registration was for HBPCL' s Animal House at Parel, Mumbai. 
The ASVS is manufactured at Pimpri, Pune, where its horse farm is located. 
For registration of this farm with CPCSEA an application was made on 
8.1.2001. Thereafter the inspections were carried out by CPCSEA. Suggestions 
 
42 

[6 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
made by them were implemented by HBPCL. However, the registration of 
HBPCL was not given on the grounds that the Institute is not following the 
prescribed guidelines in the production of Anti-Snake Venom Serum. On 
29.3.2001, the Member Secretary, CPCSEA directed HBPCL to suspend 
production of ASVS, which was complied with by HBPCL. Since monsoon 
was approaching, a shortage of this life saving drug was apprehended and the 
Government of Maharashtra advised HBPCL to resume production of ASVS. 
Accordingly, HBPCL resumed production of ASVS from 30.5.2001 onwards 
and the fact was informed to the Government of Maharashtra and CPCSEA. 
Since the Food and Drug Administration, Government of Maharashtra, has 
not sent any proposal for suspension/cancellation of ASVS manufactured by 
HBPCL to the Drug Controller General of India, who is the Central Licensing 
Approval Authority (CLAA), has neither cancelled nor suspended the 
production of ASVS production by HBPCL. 
The Government of Maharashtra has also decided to form a high level 
committee of experts to review various aspects regarding management of 
enquines in Anti-Snake Venom Serum production in Pune. The State 
Government has informed the Ministry  of Social Justice & Empowerment 
that it is committed to prevent cruelty to animals.

Statement 
The details of the procedure being followed for disinvestment of PSUs 
 Proposals  for disinvestment  in  any  PSU,  based  on  the 
recommendations of the Disinvestment Commission or in accordance 
with the declared Disinvestment Policy of the Government, are placed 
for consideration of the Cabinet Committee on Disinvestment (CCD).  
 
48 

[6 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
 After CCD clears Ihe disinvestment proposal, selection of the Advisors 
for assisting in the implementation of the disinvestment decision, is 
done through a competitive bidding process. 
 The Advisors assist the Governme nt in preparation and issue of 
advertisement in leading newspapers/magazines/journals, for inviting 
Expression of Interest (EOI) from prospective Strategic Partners. In 
cases of urgency, EOI is prepared by Department of Disinvestment 
and issued after approval of Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG). 
 After receipt of the EOI, Prospec tive Bidders are short listed, based 
on objective screening in the light of the announced pre- qualification 
criteria/requirements. 
 The Advisors, after due diligence of the PSU, prepare the Information 
Memorandum in consultation with the concerned PSU. This is given 
to the short listed Prospective Bidders, who have entered into a 
Confidentiality Agreement. 
 The draft Share Purchase Agreement or the Shareholders Agreement 
are also prepared by the Advisors, with the help of the Legal Advisors, 
and given to the Prospective Bidders for eliciting their reaction. 
 The Prospective Bidders undertake due diligence of the PSU and hold 
discussions with the Advisors/the Government/the representatives of 
the PSU for any clarifications. 
 Concurrently, the task of valuation of the PSU is undertaken in 
accordance with the standard national and international practices. 
 Based on the reactions received from the Prospective Bidders, the 
Share Purchase Agreement and Shareholders Agreement are finalised 
and after vetting by the Ministry of Law, they are approved by the 
Govemment. Thereafter, they are sent to the Prospective Bidders for 
inviting the final binding bids {Technical and Financial). 
 After examination, analysis and evaluation of the bids, the 
recommendations of the Inter Mi nisterial Group (IMG) are placed 
before the CCD for a final decision regarding selection of the 
Strategic Partner, signing of the Share Purchase & Shareholders 
Agreements and other ancillary issues. 
 In the disinvestment process mentioned above. Department of 
Disinvestment is assisted at each State by an Inter Ministerial Group 
(IMG) comprising officers from the Ministry of Finance, Department 
of Public Enterprises, the Administrative Ministry/ Department

the Department of Disinvestment and the Advisors. 
 After the transaction is completed, all papers and documents relating 
to it shall be turned over the Comptroller and Auditor General of 
India; the CAG shall prepare an evaluation for sending to Parliament 
and releasing to the public.

Examination of Samatha case regarding mining lease 
before disinvestment of BALCO 
1523. DR. BIPLAB DASGUPTA: Will the Miniser of DISINVESTMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Supreme Court had decided in the Samatha case against giving 
the mining lease of Government land in scheduled areas to non-tribals; 
(b) whether this judgement was kepi in view and its implications critically 
examined before taking the disinvestment decision of BALCO; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE  DEPARTMENT OF 
DISINVESTMET (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) The Samatha judgement 
57 

RAJYA SABHA [6 August, 2001 ] 
had interpreted the Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Areas Land Transfer 
Regulations, 1959, and held that any tran sfer of land in the areas notified as 
per the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution (Scheduled Areas) in favour of 
non-tribals on mining lease was void in Andhra Pradesh. The Samatha 
judgement also gave certain  direction to be followed by other States that had 
areas notified under the Fifth Schedule. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) and (d) In the State of Chhattisgarh (or the erstwhile State of Madhya 
Pradesh), necessary Regulations have not been made by the State Government 
under para 5(2) the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution, as was done in Andhra 
Pradesh. The Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959 also docs not ban 
the transfer of land by way of a leas e. Besides, land allotted to BALCO 
continues to remain with BALCO. As such, disinvestment in BALCO is not 
attracted by Samatha Judgement. As they have been challenged, all these issues 
are pending before the Hon'ble Supreme Court.

OFFICE MEMORANDUM 
Subject: Guidlines for qualification of Advisors for disinvestment 
process 
Govemment has examined the issu e of framing comprehensive and 
transparent guidelines defining the criteria for selection of Advisors, so that 
the parties selected through competitiv e bidding inspire public confidence. 
Earlier, a set of criteria like sector experience, knowledge, commitment etc. 
use to be prescribed. Based on experience and in consultation with concerned 
departments, Government has decided to prescribe the following additional 
criteria for the qualification/disqualificatio n of the parties to act as Advisors 
to the Government for the disinvestment transactions:— 
(a) Any cpnviction by a Court of Law or indictment/adverse order by a 
regulatory authority for a grave offenc e against the Advising concern or its 
sister concern would constitute a disqualification. Grave offence would be 
defined to bc'of such a nature that it outrages the moral sense of the community. 
The decision in regard to the nature of offence would be taken on a case to 
case basis after considering the facts of the case and relevant legal principles by 
the Government. Similarly, the decision in regard to the relationship between the 
sister concerns would be taken, based on relevant facts and after examining 
whether the two concerns are substantially controlled by the same person/ 
persons. 
(b) In case such a disqualification takes place, after the entity has already 
been appointed as Advisor, the party would be under an obligation to widraw 
voluntarily from the disinvestment process, failing which the Government would 
have the liberty to terminate the appointment/contract. 
(c) Disqualification shall continue fo r a period that Government deems 
appropriate. 
60 

[6 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) Any entity, which is disqualified from participating in the disinvestment 
process, would not be allowed to remain associated with it or get associated 
merely because it has preferred an app eal against the order based on which it 
has been disqualified. The mere pendency of appeal will have no effect on the 
disqualification. 
(e) The disqualification criteria would co me into effect immediately and 
would apply to all the Advisors already appointed by the Government for 
various disinvestment transactions, which have not yet been completed. 
(f) Before disqualifying a concern, a Show Cause Notice why it should not 
disqualified would be issued to it and it would be given an opportunity to 
explain its position. 
(g) Henceforth, these criteria will be prescribed in the advertisements seeking 
Expressions of Interest (EOI) from the interested parties to act as Advisor. 
Further, the interested parties shall be required to provide with their EOI an 
undertaking to the effect that no investigation by a regulatory authority is 
pending against them. In case any investigation is pending against the concern 
or its sister concern or against the CEO or any of its directors/Managers/ 
Employees, full details of such investigation including the name of the 
investigating agency, the charge/offence for which the investigation has been 
launched, name and designation of persons against whom the investigation 
has been launched and other relevant in formation should be disclosed, to the 
satisfaction of the Government. For other criteria also, similar undertaking 
will be obtained along with EOI. They would also have to give an undertaking 
that if they are disqualified as per the prescribed criteria, at any time before the 
transaction is completed, they would be required to inform the Government of 
the same and voluntarily withdraw from the assignment. 
(h) The interested parties would also be required to give an undertaking 
that there exists no conflict of interest as on the date of their appointment as 
Advisors in handling of the transaction and that, in future, if such a conflict of 
interest arises, the Advisor would immediately intimate the Government of the 
same. For disinvestment proposes, 'conflict of interest' is defined to include 
engaging in any activity or business by the Advisor in association with any 
third Party, during the engagement, which would or may be reasonably expected 
to, directly or indirectly, materially adversely affect the interest of Government 
of India or the Company (being disinvested) in relation to the transaction, and 
in respect of which the Advisor has or may obtain any proprietary or confidential 
information during the engagement, that, if known to any other client of the

Advisor, could be used in any manner by such client to the material 
disadvantage of Government of India or the Company (being disinvested) in 
the transaction. The conflict of interest would be deemed to have arisen if any 
Advisor firm/concern, has any professional or commercial relationship with 
any bidding firm/concern for the same disinvestment transaction during the 
pendency of such transaction. In this context, both Advisor firm and bidding 
firm would mean the distinct and separate legal entities and would not include 
their sister concern, group concern or  affiliates etc. The professional or 
commercial relationship is defined to include acting on behalf of the bidder or 
undertaking any assignment for the bidder of any nature, whether or not directly 
related to disinvestment transaction. 
(i) On receiving information on conflict of interest, the Government would 
give the option to the Advisor to either eliminate the conflict of interest within 
a stipulated time or withdraw from the transaction and the Advisor would be 
required to act accordingly, failing which Government would have the liberty 
to terminate the appointment/contract.

Statement 
The details of the procedure being followed for disinvestment of PSUs 
 Proposals for disinvestment in any PSU, based on the 
recommendations of the Disinvestment Commission or in accordance 
with the declared Disinvestment Policy of the Government, are placed 
for consideration of the Cabinet Committee on Disinvestment (CCD). 
 AfterCCD clears the disinvestment proposal, selection of the Advisors 
for assisting in the implementation of the disinvestment decision, is 
done through a competitive bidding process. 
 The Advisors assist the Governme nt in preparation and issue of 
advertisement in leading newspapers/magazines/journals, for inviting 
Expression of Interest (EOI) from prospective Strategic Partners. In 
cases of urgency, EOI is prepared by Department of Disinvestment 
and issued after approval of Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG). 
 After receipt of the EOI, Prospective Bidders are short listed, based 
 
64 

[6 August, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
on objective screening in the light of the announced pre qualification 
criteria/requirements. 
 The Advisors, after due diligence of the PSU, prepare the information 
Memorandum in consultation with the concerned PSU. This is given to 
the short listed Prospective Bidde rs, who have entered into a 
Confidentiality Agreement. 
 The draft Share Purchase Agreement or the Shareholders Agreement 
are also prepared by the Adviso rs, with the help of the Legal 
Advisors, and given to the Prospective Bidders for eliciting their 
reaction. 
 The Prospective Bidders undertake due diligence of the PSU and 
hold discussions with the Advisors/the Government/the representatives of 
the PSU for any clarifications'. 
 Concurrently, the task of valuation of the PSU is undertaken in 
accordance with the standard national and international practices. 
 Based on the reactions received from the Prospective Bidders, the Share 
Purchase Agreement and Shareholders Agreement are finalised and 
after vetting by the Ministry of Law, they are approved by the 
Government. Thereafter, they are sent to the Prospective Bidders for 
inviting the final binding bids (Technical and Financial). 
 After examination, analysis and evaluation of the bids, the 
recommendations of the Inter Ministerial Group (IMG) are placed before 
the CCD for a final decision regarding selection of the Strategic Partner, 
signing of the Share Purchase & Shareholders Agreements and other 
ancillary issues. 
 In the disinvestment process mentioned above. Department of 
Disinvestment is assisted at each stage by an Inter Ministerial Group 
(IMG) comprising officers from the Ministry of Finance, Department of 
Public Enterprises, the Administrative Ministry/ Department 
controlling the PSU, the PSU concerned apart from the officers of the 
Department of Disinvestment and the Advisors. 
 After the transaction is completed, all papers and documents relating to it 
shall be turned over the Comptroller and Auditor General of India; the 
CAG shall prepare an evaluation for sending to Parliament and releasing to 
the public.

Visit by Minister abroad 
1592. SHRI SATISH PR ADHAN: Will the Minist er of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) the countries visited by her predecessor/her during the last two years; and 
(b) the details of achievements of those visit, country-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) The requisite information is given 
in the enclosed statement. 
Statement 
Foreign visits of Minister and of her predecessor 
Shri Arun Jaitley, the then Minister of State of Information and Broadcasting visited 
Syria and Dubai from 28th January to 1st February, 2000 during which Cultural 
Exchange Programme between India and Syria and the Protocol on Cooperation in 
the sphere of TV and Radio broadcasting was reviewed. 
Shri Arun Jaitley also visited London (United Kingdom) from 6th to 9th 
February, 2000 to attend a Special International Seminar on Convergence and 
Broadcasting Regulations. 
Smt. Sushma Swaraj, Information and Broadcasting Minister visited France and 
UK from 13th May to 19th May, 2001. As a result of her meeting with the French 
Minister for Culture and Communications, both countries agreed on setting up on a 
Sub-Group on films under the aegis of the Indo-French Forum. The visit also 
included a stopover at the ongoing Cannes Film Market where India had set up an 
Indian Pavilion, for the first time, to promote Indian films and software by providing 
a common platform for all Indian participants to interact with their counterparts 
from various countries. Her visit to Cannes focused media attention on the Indian 
Pavilion and on Indian films. In London, the Minister visited Institutions connected 
with fitm and broadcasting industries, 
142 

[6 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
including the BBC. The experience of BBC, as a public broadcaster, was 
discussed in order to get inputs for policy-making in the realm of Public Broadcast 
in India. 
Smt. Sushma Swaraj, Minister of Information and Broadcasting visited 
Japan, USA and UK from 12th June to 22nd June, 2001. As a Leader of the 
delegation of the top captains of Indian Entertainment Industry (brought 
together by FICCI), she visited Japan and USA.'Somc of the immediate 
achievements are: (i) the possibility of more Indian films being released in 
Japan, with the NHK considering to increase the number of Indian films 
screened by them (ii) talks have been initiated by Indian companies with their 
Japanese counterparts for doing animation work in I n d i a  (iii) an increased 
interest evinced by US companies and International Finance Corporation 
(IFC) in funding the media and broadcast sectors (iv) an offer of assistance 
from Motion Picture Association of Amer ica (MPA) to help curb piracy of 
Indian films in the US. In addition, the members of the delegation got 
extensive opportunity to interact with their overseas counterparts. 
In UK, the Minister held discussions with Regulator for Telecommunications 
Industries (OFTEL) which provided us eful inputs for setting up similar 
institutions in India, in the light of convergence technology.

1623. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of SHIPPING be 
pleased to state:

an increase in the Gross Registered Tonnage (GRT) of Indian Shipping during 
the Ninth Plan period;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING (SHRI 
HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (b) Yes Sir. 
The Government has taken several steps to increase the Gross Registered 
Tonnage (GRT) of the Indian Shipping during the Ninth five year plan period. 
The steps taken are as under:— 
(i) Shipping companies have been allowed to retain sale proceeds of their 
ships abroad and utilise them for fresh acquisition; 
(ii) The Shipping companies are now permitted to get ther ships repaired 
in any shipyard without seeking prior approval from the Government; 
(iii) Indian Shipping Companies can now time charter-out ships; 
(iv) No permission is required for raising foreign exchange loans from 
abroad by mortgaging the vessel with the lender; 
(v) Section 33 AC of Income Tax Act has been restored in its original 
form, thereby facilitating ploughing back of profits by Shipping 
Companies for new acquisition. 
166 

[6 August, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(vi) The provisions of "EXIM POLICY " relating to import of vessels has 
been amended w.e.f. 1.4.2001 bringing all category of vessels/ships 
under OGL and thereby dispensing  with licence requirement for 
import of various kinds ships. Ships could now be imported freely 
without licence. 
(vii) The Depreciation rate on ships has been enhanced from 20% to 25% 
w.e.f. 1.4.2001, thereby facilitating faster tonnage replacement. 
(viii) 100% Foregin Direct Investment in Shipping Sector is permitted. 
Due to facilitative steps taken by the Government as mentioned above, the 
Shipping Companies have been able to acquire 115 Ships of various types, 
which include 33 new built vessels during the period 1.4.97 to 31.3.2001. 
Further, The Shipping Corporation of India has already placed orders for 8 
new vessels and has proposals to acquire more vessels during this year. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. Priority is being accorded to modernisation and

on several waterways identified for undertaking such expansion;

HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes, Sir: 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) Three waterways have been declared  as national waterways.These are 
as under: National Waterway No. I—Allahabad-Haldia stretch (1620 
Km) of Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly river System.

navigability of the following waterways have been conducted.

Juvenile Homes 
1628. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Juvenile Justice Act is not good for children 
and juvenile homes are over-crowded; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that recen tly the upper age limit of children in 
homes has been increased from 16 to 18 in a convention held in Delhi; and 
(c) if so, the steps being taken by Government to redraft the Act as also to 
increase the number and capacity of juvenile homes? 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [6 August, 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The Govemment is not aware of any Convention held in Delhi 
recommending increase of age in the Juvenile Justice Act. However, the 
Government has already replaced the Juvenile Justice Act, 1986 by a new Act 
namely, The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000. 
This Act has been enforced in the country except the State of Jammu & Kashmir 
with effect from I st April, 2001. As per the new Act uniform age of 18 years has 
been prescribed for both boys and girls under the Juvenile Justice Act, which 
was earlier 16 years for boys and 18 years for girls. The Central Government is 
implementing a scheme called "A programme for Juvenile Justice", under which 
the State Governments and Union Territory Administrations arc assisted on a 
50:50 basis for establishing and running of Homes under the Juvenile Justice 
Act. The Homes arc being administer ed by the State Governments and UT 
Administrations. They arc required to send proposals for availing the grants 
under this scheme. Whenever, proposals arc received from State Governments/ 
UT Administrations for establishment of new Homes or expansion of cxising 
ones, the grants arc released by the Central Government to them for the purpose 
as per norms.

schemes and actual money spent by the State Governments during the last 
financial year; 
(c) the reasons for the delay in implementation of schemes and utilisation 
of funds; and 
(d) the steps proposed for proper utilisation of funds?

[6 August, 200I ] RAJYA SABHA

EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI): (a) lo (d) Under the 
strategy of Special Component Plan (SCP) evolved by the Planning 
Commission, the State Governments arc required to make SCP by earmarking a 
percentage of Plan fund in proportion to the percentage pf SC population in the 
State. Fund provided under SCP is utilized on implementation of different schemes 
for welfare of the notified SC communities of the State including the Nav-Buddhas. 
Details on scheme-wise amount allocated and utilized by the State Government under 
the SCP is maintained by the State Government concerned. 
Implementation of SCP and overfall flow of fund to SCP is looked into by the 
Central Government while earmarking 25% of the Special Central Assistance, 
which is provided as an additive to the SCP. Followings steps arc being taken by

illegal adoption homes in the country?

AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI MANEKA GANDHI): (a) After 
reports from Andhra Pradesh about some irregularities, the Union Government 
has issued directives to all State Governments to take stringent action against 
organizations indulging in illegal activities in the field of adoptions. 
(b) to (d) Though no separate letter has been written to the State Home 
Ministers, all the State Governments have  been asked to take necessary steps 
to prevent similar incidents in future which inter alia, include: 
(i) Licensing of all Residential Homes and setting up of a state adoption 
unit. (ii) Joint inspections should take place of orphanages and agencies. 
(iii) Enforcement of Orphanages and other Charitable Homes Act, 1960. 
(iv) Monitoring of adoption activities quoting recent happenings in Andhra 
Pradesh.

organizations to streamling their activities and adhere to the Government 
guidelines in this respect.

1637. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are satisfied with the financial performance of 
steel sector in the country; 
(b) if so, the financial position of the public sector steel units; 
(c) how these compare with those operating in the private sector; and 
(d) the measures taken by Government to improve the financial position of 
steel units? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STEEUSHRI BRAJ 
KISHORE TRIPATHY): (a) to (c) The performance of public sector steel plants 
i.e. Steel Authority of India Limited(SAIL) and Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited, 
(RINL) has been satisfactory. Government docs not monitor the performance 
of private sector steel plants. SAIL has reduced its losses from Rs. 1720 crore 
in 1999-2000 to Rs.720 crore (Provisional) in 2000-01,representing a reduction 
in losses of about 58%. The financial performance of RINL during the year

restructuring package for SAIL to improve its financial position. 
Production of indigenous steel 
† 1638. SHRI GOPALSIN H G. SOLANKI: Will the Minister of STEEL 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the extent of success achieved in the production of indigenous steel 
uptil now; 
(b) the extent to which the indigenous steel is capable of meeting the demand 
of steel in the country; 
(c) whether Government have formulated any scheme for providing 
incentives to the domestic steel producers so that they can meet the target; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI BRAJ 
KISHORE TRIPATHY): (a) the Indian iron and steel industry was the first 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [6 August, 2001] 
core sector lo be fully deregulated in 1991-92. Post liberalization, the Indian 
iron and sleel industry achieved very high growth rate. The production of 
finished sleel increased from 15.2 million tonnes in 1992-93 to 29.7 (prov.) 
million tonnes in 2000-01. The apparent steel consumption has increased from 
18.66 million tonnes in 1994-95 to 26.6 million tonnes in 2000-01. Export of 
iron and steel has increased for 0.9 million tonnes in 1992-93 to over 3 million 
tonnes in 2000-01. Today, India is the ninth largest steel producer in the world 
and a net exporter of steel. Indian steel industry is capable of producing almost 
all grades, sizes and excellent quality of steel products. Earlier, exports consisted 
mainly of plates, bars and rods and structural, whereas, now semis, hot rolled 
coils, cold rolled coils, pig iron and sponge iron are also being exported. Indian 
steel is exported lo many countries of the world including China, Japan, USA, 
Korea, Taiwan, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Italy, U.K. Germany, Canada, 
Spain, Australia, etc. However, the mo st notable achievement of the Indian 
steel industry is its integration with the global economy. 
(b) The indigenous sleel industry is fully capable of meeting the entire 
demand of steel in the country. 
(c) and (d) The Govemment of India has not formulated any specific scheme 
for providing incentives to the domestic steel producers. However, several steps 
have been taken to boost the production and demand for steel in the country. 
These inter-alia include, upgradation of technology, modernization of public 
sector steel plants for improvement in quality and productivity, encouragement 
to research and development, facilitating adoption of cost effective and state-
of-the-art technologies, higher allocation for infrastructure development to boost 
the demand for steel etc.
